speakeroldname: Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it is appropriate that at this time I should outline some of the views of the government on the matter of immigration. Canada is a nation of immigrants, and immigration policy has always been a prime concern of Canadian governments. Since June,
1957	this government has been carefully reviewing immigration legislation, policy and administration; not to make changes for the sake of change alone, but to arrive at some basic principles upon which to build a national immigration policy. I believe that as a result of the experience we have gained we are now approaching the point where we should be able to offer to the house specific proposals which will translate desirable principles into legislative form.
Already, of course, during the past few years a number of significant changes in policy and in administrative procedures have been made. Some of the most important steps taken by this government have been as follows:
1.	One of our first moves after taking office was to change the regulation which had formerly prevented Canadian residents of Asian origin from sponsoring the admission of their spouses and children until they became Canadian citizens.
2.	Next, the immigration appeal board was strengthened and its scope expanded.
3.	A new policy governing temporary residents of Canada was announced in August,
1958	which made it possible to regularize the status of several thousands of persons who had previously entered the country on a nonimmigrant basis.
4.	In co-operation with the provinces, significant improvements were made in measures providing for the welfare of immigrants after arrival.
5.	Another important change, which I announced to the house only last month,

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration simplified the arrangements by which residents of Canada may bring fiancees to this country. This beneficial change affects particularly Chinese and Japanese residents by freeing them from the necessity of posting large cash bonds before their fiancees can come forward.
Canada needs immigrants for many reasons, the most obvious of which is to provide skills and training necessary for the development of the country. Less apparent to many Canadians are the other immediate and long range advantages of immigration which I would like to summarize as follows:
1.	We need a steady flow of immigrants to balance and offset emigration from the country, which, although decreasing, is still substantial.
2.	Many immigrants bring productive capital to Canada, and establish businesses and enterprises which employ Canadian as well as immigrant workers.
3.	A small population in a large country results in a high per capita cost of maintaining transportation and communications facilities, defence and many other public services. Population growth, through natural increase and through immigration, helps to offset this.
4.	As our population grows, the resulting expansion of the domestic market encourages the attraction and development of units of production which cannot be based economically on a far-flung, low-density market.
5.	A steadily growing consumers' market in Canada, reinforced by immigration, reduces this country's dependence on imports and exports, and consequently makes our economy less sensitive to economic fluctuations outside our borders.
6.	New population stimulates economic, cultural and social activity, and makes possible for old and new Canadians alike the achievement of a higher level of cultural independence and creativity.
These are some of the reasons from Canada's own point of view why we need to continue to encourage a steady flow of suitable immigrants to this country. There are, of course, other considerations as well which we must also take into account, among them being our relationships with other countries and our responsibilities as a member of the larger international community.
How then do we proceed to develop an immigration policy and program which will reflect in practical fashion the various considerations I have just outlined? Obviously we cannot simply go ahead and bring to this country everyone who may wish to migrate, without regard to possible effects on our Canadian people or on the immigrants

themselves. Canada, it seems to me, has a responsibility to admit newcomers in accordance with our ability to provide opportunities for them and the capacity of our society to integrate them socially and economically.
Since we cannot take all those who might wish to live in Canada, we should admit those who are able to make a positive contribution to Canadian life, not simply in economic terms but in terms of what the immigrants can be expected to add to the variety and attractiveness of our society. The number of immigrants we can take at any one time will depend upon the rate of development in Canada and the capacity of our various levels of government to deal with the many problems arising from growth-The government aims at a policy of vigorous national development which will create new opportunities, not only for Canadians but also for those who will join us as immigrants.
Against the background of these larger considerations of national development policy it becomes clear that whatever may have been the practices and policies of earlier decades, we can no longer trust to chance to bring immigrants to our shores without counsel or guidance. We must continue by every reasonable means to develop and maintain a substantial flow of highly suitable immigrants, and at the same time avoid haphazard or arbitrary stimulations or restrictions of that flow, in other words the sudden turning on and off of the immigration tap which on occasion has given rise to difficulties in the past.
Immigrants coming to Canada must be prepared for what they will face here and be ready to properly accept their responsibilities and exercise their rights in Canadian life. Immigrants should be encouraged to go to those areas in Canada in which new population is most needed and where opportunities exist, rather than to congregate in the already overcrowded areas. It should at all times be our policy to take those measures which are necessary to ensure the prompt and effective integration into Canadian society of those whom we admit. This will be to the advantage of all Canadians, as well as promoting the unity of Canada itself.
It is of course the prerogative of Canada to decide who is to be admitted as an immigrant. No one has an absolute right to demand admission. If the government is to carry out an energetic, forward-looking immigration program, decisions must be made and the government must be able to decide in the interest of Canada which immigrants will be admitted and which rejected.
The administration must be able to choose from among available applicants those who

will be most suitable to life in Canada. We shall do our best to admit as immigrants individuals and families who are personally suitable and who have the required background and training to become worth-while citizens. This must be done on the basis of a system of selection which is fair and just, which will bring to Canada those settlers whom we need and who can become settled in our communities without dislocation to our way of life or hardship to the immigrants themselves.
In summary, what we are endeavouring to do is to develop an immigration program in which movements are properly planned, and we therefore avoid situations where arbitrary administrative action is required. In this way it should be possible to convince worth-while settlers that Canada is genuinely and continuously interested in receiving them and helping to find a place for them within our society. To ensure this result it is essential that the Canadian public, and prospective immigrants as well, should be assured that our policy is not a rigid but a flexible one, based on a consistent framework of principle, subject to continuing intelligent supervision, and capable of adjustment to meet the changing needs of a dynamic and growing country.
The key to our immigration policy will be the consistent application of proper selection standards designed to bring the best possible settlers to Canada. I am sure all Canadians would agree that once these standards are established they should be applied consistently to all who seek admission to this country, except where the admission of the immigrant is based on compassionate grounds or on close relationship; and, of course, in the case of refugees. Other immigrants, particularly those who will earn their living in Canada and compete in the Canadian labour market, will be examined to determine that they will be able to make their living successfully in Canada, that they will be likely to become good Canadian citizens, and that their admission will not result in disruptions in Canadian social and economic life. We shall, of course, continue to place strong emphasis on the selection of immigrants who will establish productive enterprises in Canada which will create employment for themselves and for Canadians.
A program conceived and developed along the lines I have outlined will, I am sure, bring results of lasting benefit not only to future immigrants themselves but to all of Canada.

As for the statement of the general principles upon which our immigration policy is based, the hon. lady might just as well have saved herself the trouble of original composition and read the excellent statement which Mr. Mackenzie King made in this house on May 1, 1947; because she has not deviated in any single particular that I can discover from any aspect of that statement.
I must say that in view of the harsh and indeed brutal criticism to which I was subjected during the three years I held the portfolio which the hon. lady now holds, it is perhaps understandable that I should take a little satisfaction in the fact that the government has, substantially, found nothing to improve on in what they found when they took office. I think this is particularly important, and especially true, in view of some of the opinions expressed by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice when they were sitting on this side of the house.
I am interested that the hon. lady should have asserted as emphatically as she did this fundamental principle that it is the prerogative of the government and parliament of this country and of no one else to decide who shall be admitted to our shores. I do not quarrel with that view at all. I have always upheld it, and I do not see how it would be possible to take any other view and expect to get the support of the Canadian people for it. But I may say there was a time when the previous administration was attacked for taking that view.

I am glad to note this agreement from now on between the two sides of the house on this fundamental point, because everything really stems from it.
I took note concerning those changes which the hon. lady stated she had made in the regulations or the administration, and later on I will say something about them. She gave five or six examples, and I took them down as well as I could. But I think the hon. lady made a mistake about one of them. It was probably only a slip of the tongue, but I do think the matter is important. She said something about the regulations having been changed to permit Canadian residents rather than Canadian citizens of Asian origin to apply for relatives. I think the hon. lady meant to say "Canadian citizens who have origins in certain countries" because if she will look at the regulations as they were amended on May 24, 1956, she will see that since that date there has not been anything in the Canadian law or regulations about the racial origin of immigrants. Since 1956, when the regulations were amended as a result of the decision in the Brent case, the question of who might apply, the categories of persons who might apply, has been a purely geographical one. In the case, let us say, of a % citizen of China who is being applied for, it does not matter whether that person is of Chinese or French or English origin; no matter what he may be, if he is a citizen of China the same law applies to him.

I think the hon. gentleman misunderstood me. It is true today that the sponsor in Canada has the right to apply


whether he is a Canadian citizen or a landed immigrant. I think the hon. gentleman himself, when he held this post, made some alterations which had to do with five years of residence rather than the applicant being a Canadian citizen.

My whole point is that if the hon. lady was using the word "Asian" in a geographical sense, I am sure she was right; if she was using it in a racial sense, it was wrong. I do think that this was an important ' change which was made on May 24, 1956. All Canadians should be glad that this change was made. It was one of the few things I did when I was minister which received commendation from the opposition.
I notice that a lot of articles are still loosely written saying people are penalized because of their race. That is no longer true in any rational sense of the term. It is true that there are certain countries from which we encourage immigration and other countries from which we do not encourage it. I do not really believe that the vast majority of the Canadian people would want that kind of principle of selection changed, though they might wish some changes made within the categories; and changes are, in fact, made from time to time. But it seems to me that is a really fundamental change that was made which we should be glad was made and which I think it is very important to emphasize at all stages.
What I really want to devote most of my time to is something which has happened very recently about which I am very critical both of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and the Minister of Justice. I refer to the investigation which, as we learn from information that comes to us from outside the house but about which we can get extraordinarily little information inside the house, is being carried on into the Chinese immigration that has taken place since the war.
I have in my hand a very detailed press report from the Vancouver Sun of May 24 last which purports to give an interview with Commissioner Harvison of the R.C.M.P. I do not intend to put this on the record. I am sure all hon. members who are really interested in this matter have read it, and I think many of them have been very much shocked by the information contained in that interview. There was also, as hon. members know because it has been alluded to already in the house, an article in the Toronto Globe and Mail on May 25 written and dispatched from Ottawa on May 24 by Mr. Langevin Cote, their correspondent here, from

which I want to read one paragraph because it seems to me it is very important. It reads as follows:
It has been reported that as many as 11,000 Chinese of 23,000 who have come to Canada since 1946 have entered the country illegally. R.C.M.P. commissioner C. W. Harvison, to whom this estimate was attributed, said the figure was not his but that he would not disagree with it.
The Minister of Justice said on Monday, I think it was, that this figure was not the official figure of the R.C.M.P. The press report does not suggest that it was the official figure of the R.C.M.P. But I feel that the government has made a very great mistake in not having the Prime Minister or some other minister come into the house and make a statement about this matter as authoritative as it would be possible to give in the circumstances. I think it is very unfortunate that anything was said about this investigation until the police were in a position to lay charges against those people, if there are any, with respect to whom there were grounds to lay such charges. I have no doubt that such an extensive investigation as this appears to be is going to result eventually in some charges being laid. If not it is going to be a most shocking waste of public funds.
But the situation we are faced with at the present time is that the 23,000 Chinese who have come into this country as immigrants, pratically, although not quite, all of whom have come here allegedly as the sons or daughters or wives of Canadian citizens or more recently of Canadian residents, though I would imagine the number in the latter category would be relatively small, find themselves in the position that a cloud of suspicion hangs over all of them and over all their relatives, which virtually means over the whole Chinese Canadian community. It does seem to me that it should have been possible to remove that cloud before now.
I have had a good deal of experience with these matters, and I do not want to say anything here that will be in any way irresponsible. I do know, as a fact, that certain irregularities did occur, because of information subsequently turned up in one or two cases that came to my attention. I would not be able to mention those cases now without access to the departmental files, because I probably have nothing in my own files. I do recall a case where a Chinese was admitted to this country who alleged that he was 18 years old. It subsequently turned out that he was really 25 years old, but he was still the son of the person he represented himself to be. I also know there have been cases where children of Chinese Canadian citizens have alleged that they were unmarried so as 79951-0-297

But the circumstances were not ordinary. We know that for many years there was a statute of this country called the Chinese immigration act, which is one of the few things in the record of the Liberal party of which I, as a Liberal, am not very proud. It had the effect of bringing about the separation of families of immigrants to Canada of Chinese origin. In the year 1947 that act was repealed and the present regime was established, and in order to undo the very unfortunate effects of that act various steps have been taken.
I am not going into the full history of that now but the purpose was to provide, as quickly as it might be done, for the reunion of families, to admit the wives of persons who became Canadian citizens and therefore indicated they wished to stay in this country, and to admit their unmarried children. The only reason that admission was confined to unmarried children was, of course, that a chain of immigration would have been set up that would have been very hard to control because of the lack of facilities of any kind that could be made available in China to provide accurate information.
This problem was subsequently very greatly complicated by the fact that, though there was no war between China and Canada, from 1950 to 1953 Chinese troops were fighting Canadian soldiers in Korea. During all that time the government of this country admitted Chinese immigrants; it is true there was only a limited number of persons from China admitted because of the relationship. In order to have any kind of control and any reasonable certainty about the identity of these persons there had to be a relatively strict regime, and that is why there was. When one thinks that it was perhaps almost unique in modern history that immigrants should be admitted to one country from another country when the troops of that country were fighting our troops, one can say that it was an example of liberality, toleration and good sense of which I think Canadians have every right to be proud and in which I personally am very proud to have had some part, although the major credit goes to Mr. Mackenzie King, Mr. St. Laurent and Mr. Walter Harris, who had the most to do with the problem and the maintenance of that policy during the critical period.
As I say, in order to make sure, particularly once the communist regime was established in China, that our limited immigration was not permitted to become an avenue for the
4716	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration back door infiltration of communist agents-I said this as early as 1955 in the committee on estimates, as I am sure the Minister of Justice will recall-it was felt by the government responsible at that time and has been felt by the present government since that these controls had to be maintained.
Now, I must say I could never find it in my heart to blame very much those applicants who represented themselves as being single when they were in fact married, or who represented their age as being something other than it was. You may say, why do we not change the regulations and let all the married applicants in? I have tried to explain that. You would have an insuperable problem in doing that because the married ones, in turn, would have children, and the opportunities for illegal entry would be vastly increased, as I am sure the hon. lady would agree.
I am going to recommend to the government, and I am doing this without seeking to be unduly critical, that many of the problems they now have as a result of this investigation could very easily be removed if the minister, the Minister of Justice or the Prime Minister would say, on behalf of the government, that the government has no intention whatever of opening any case or dealing with any case where those people who entered were the sons, daughters, wives or parents of 'Canadian citizens of Chinese origin, even though they may have misrepresented some of the other facts for which the department asked.
If a categorical statement of that sort could be made that this was not, after all, considered so serious as to necessitate the reopening of these cases, I believe most of the uneasiness and concern in the Chinese Canadian community would be ended at once. I believe that until that is done there is not the slightest real hope, if one is going to be realistic about it, of getting any information from anyone or any real co-operation from anyone in the Chinese Canadian community in assisting in the investigation.
I do believe there are a good many people in the Chinese Canadian community who have been victimized. I said as early as 1956, when I was questioned on this-I brought the reference here in case anyone wants me to repeat it, but I do not believe it is necessary-that although I had no proof in any particular case I was quite sure there had been a number of fraudulent entries. I was afraid, because there are no reliable vital statistics in China and because of other difficulties in respect of this immigration, that there were a few people slipping through all the time. I am sure there have been cases where people have been blackmailed. I feel


sure that there are people in the Chinese Canadian community who would like to assist in having this practice stopped, but I do not believe it is reasonable to expect that they will do anything about it if they believe the result is going to be to bring reprisals or bring any kind of action against the relatives of Chinese Canadian citizens who have come here in a technically illegal sense.
I am seeking, therefore, to criticize as little as possible, because I know from my experience that this matter is very difficult. I have not forgotten the way I was assailed in 1955, when I had had very little experience in this department, because I refused, as I believe the present minister would refuse to show certain people the departmental files on these cases so they could get, as I suspected some of them wanted, additional information to facilitate illegal entries. I was accused by the Prime Minister and by the Minister of Justice of being arbitrary and tyrannical because I took that position. I must say that I think I would have no choice, with any sense of responsibility, but to take it again. I have accused the minister of many things, and I am going to accuse her of many more things before I am finished. However, I am sure the minister does not want, any more than I do, to encourage the breaking of the law or to treat with inhumanity those people who may have been guilty of some technical breach but no other kind of breach.
I do say to the minister that I believe this matter should be cleared up, and cleared up at once. By that I do not mean for a moment that the investigation into genuine criminal activities should not be completed. Of course it should. If the minister finds that certain people were taking advantage of our laws and of our liberality-because when you compare the way we treat immigration from China with the way any other country in the world treats it, it is very liberal-then they should be dealt with accordingly. If these people are taking advantage of that position to bring undesirable people to North America, of course every effort should be made to stop that practice. If an effort is being made to get people into this country who ought not to be here, who are a danger to the security of Canada or the security of the free world, of course that should be stopped. If people are being blackmailed with that or any other end in view, that should be stopped. If it is true, as I have read in some of these press stories in papers like the Toronto Telegram-I do not know that I should say "papers like the Toronto Telegram"; I should say in the Toronto Telegram because perhaps there is no other paper like

it-that bribes have to be offered in order to get officials to do their duty, then that should be investigated.
I would not believe this story unless I had proof of it. I have had a lot of experience and I do not believe there is any more honest, trustworthy staff in any department in any government anywhere in the world than there is in the immigration branch. This is not to say they are not human like all the rest of us. There may occasionally be some one who is susceptible to various kinds of temptation.
I say these things should be found out, and there should be the greatest vigour in any such investigation. But I do say if this investigation is to amount to anything, if we are to get anywhere with it, it is of the utmost importance that we should make clear at once that so far as those people who are relatives of Chinese Canadian citizens are concerned, who may have committed some technical irregularity in connection with their entry, they are not going to face deportation or any other charges.
A few such cases came to my notice when I was minister. One of the ways in which they came to my notice was this. Someone who had been admitted three or four years before as a single person would then apply for the admission of his wife and children. Well, when that happened there was prima facie evidence that he had not given accurate information before. I have regarded that as one of the facts of life, if I may put it that way. There were cases where I admitted the wife and children afterwards.. As I say, it seems to me that this is the nub of the whole difficulty.
The other thing that I think is rather unfortunate is this rather extravagant publicity that seems to have been occasioned. I am not saying I directly blame the commissioner of the mounted police, but I think it would have been better if he had not given this interview at all. Once you get a headline like this, "Racketeers average $4,000 per head", and then you get statements about 11,000 so-called illegal entries, they call it a $44 million racket. Anyone can do elementary arithmetic and can see where these figures come from. No doubt there were one or two cases in which somebody spent $4,000, and then someone else said there were 11,000 cases.
You multiply the two and you get $44 million. I would greatly doubt whether all the Chinese Canadian applicants together, if they took their property, would be able to find $44 million to engage in this racket. Sometimes these stories are so manifestly absurd on their face that one wonders why people write them at all without first doing a little bit of mental arithmetic. As I said, 79951-0-2974
9, 1SSQ
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration having regard to the exaggeration in this whole matter and the indictment of a whole section of the Canadian Chinese community, which has a record for obeying the law that many of the rest of us .might envy, it seems to me that it is really of the utmost importance that this matter should be cleared up without delay.
I have a number of other things about which I want to talk but, Mr. Chairman, since one may speak as often as one can catch your eye I think I ought to yield the floor at this point to somebody else.

There are two or three matters under this particular vote upon which I would like to speak quite briefly. I must admit that I find some of the policies, the regulations and the administration of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration most confusing, and I hope the minister, during the course of the discussion of her estimates, will be able to clear away some of that confusion.
One point that I find most disturbing and am unable to understand-and I think a great many other people are in the same position -is the basis upon which the department puts out publicity in an endeavour to bring immigrants into our country. Just over a month ago, as a matter of fact during the Easter recess, when I was home in Vancouver I had the opportunity of seeing copies of newspapers from the United Kingdom and other countries containing advertisements put out by the minister's department outlining a great many things about our country and its potentialities, and then enumerating opportunities that were open in Canada for people from those countries if they desired to come here. When we have in Canada over half a million unemployed, and when we have a particularly serious situation in the construction industry, for the life of me I cannot understand why the Department of Citizen-shop and Immigration should be advertising overseas to the effect that there are openings in the same areas in which we have thousands upon thousands of unemployed. For the life of me I cannot understand that policy.
I noticed that, according to the newspapers here in Ottawa only this week, it was stated in the trades and labour council that over 50 per cent of the carpenters and construction workers of Ottawa were unemployed and had been unemployed for months. I know that in my own city of Vancouver in the construction industry we are facing a serious situation; that approximately half the carpenters, half the painters and half the electricians are unemployed and that some of them have been unemployed for almost a year, with a great many of them having run out of unemployment insurance benefits and having been cut
4718	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration off seasonal benefits. With that situation in existence, why the minister should authorize or permit advertising outside ot the country inviting carpenters, painters, electricians and concrete workers to come to Canada and saying there are openings here for them is something I do not understand. As I say, it passeth all comprehension.
When we have the statement of the Prime Minister, as reported in the press when he was in the United Kingdom recently, that we will welcome tens of thousands of new Canadians, and when we read the statement made by the minister south of the border some time ago inviting Americans to come here and enumerating certain trades in which there are thousands of unemployed in this country I say that we find the situation very confusing.
Of course we should like to have immigration, but surely it should be on a planned basis, whereby we know that the immigrants can be assimilated. Although we have this recognition of the fact that we can and will grow, and that we can eventually have a bigger population, I have no hesitation in saying that our first responsibility is to the people who are in Canada now. It is unfair to the Canadian professions and to the workers who are out of work, and it is unfair to those whom you are inviting to come here when you are doing it under false pretences.
The minister must know of the type of advertising that has been put out in the past few months and of the enumeration of trades in which it is said there are openings, and that it is just barefaced misrepresentation. I hope we can have an explanation as to why that particular policy has been adopted or why that particular type of advertising has been put out under the particular circumstances which apply in some of these trades and professions here in Canada today, which have existed for some time in the past and which, from all indications, seem likely to exist for some time in the future.
That is all I want to say on that particular phase at the moment. However, I should like to add the hope that greater care will be exercised in the investigation of those who make application to come to this country-if we are in such a position that they can be accepted-in order to see that if objection is raised to their coming it is not just on the basis of the declaration of somebody else. I think it is most unfair-and we have had this matter come to our attention on more than one occasion-that a person can be turned down, with no reason being given as to why he has been turned down.
I know I had a case-it was not under the present minister, but it illustrates my point- in which a large family consisting of some


small children and some children who were grown up, married and had their own children; the entire family-were allowed to come in and then at the last minute one son was told that he could not come. Just one out of a large group was refused admission. I think the whole family, counting in-laws and everything else, would have numbered about 26. Yet one son was told no, and he never could find out why.
This happened in my home constituency, so I took up the problem. It took me almost two years to have an investigation made as to why that one son was refused admission. He never knew and to this day he does not know why he was refused. However, the minister eventually had an investigation made, and it was found that the man had been rejected because somebody had gone to one of the field officers and said the man was a criminal. No investigation was made; the statement was just accepted. Yet we finally found out that the man had never had any criminal record whatsoever. The trouble was that the person who made the objection was sore because this man had married the girl he wanted to marry. Hence he just put in a complaint, and that one person was stopped. Eventually that individual was allowed to come to Canada. However, that is the sort of thing that has happened more than once, namely the acceptance of a statement from somebody without investigation. If that man had been told why he was rejected the matter could have been cleared up in five minutes. But no; the policy is that you must never tell when they ask. I think more care should be exercised in matters of that nature.
May I also say this, because it is in a similar vein, although perhaps the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate will not agree. I want to say that I completely understand why no person should be allowed to just go and ask for information about one individual, as to why he had been turned down, or ask for the basis on which he was allowed into this country. But when we have an individual who asks for that information himself, or who says that he would not mind having the reason a certain position was taken disclosed, then I think in the name of far-famed British justice that individual should be entitled to that information or to have it made public.
Mr. Chairman, I have never been able to understand this absolute cloak of secrecy, which can only be for one purpose-the minister has dealt with it time after time- namely for the protection of the name of the individual. But if the person concerned wants to know or wants the information made known, then why should not that be allowed?

And that is most important when tied in with what I have said previously, because I say without any hesitation that time after time the department accept what they are told and do not investigate, and they can be wrong very often. I think a person should have the opportunity, if he so desires, of being able to disprove any allegations made against him by asking for information which has been laid about him.
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?
Certainly.

Does the hon. gentleman realize that the argument he is now making is precisely the argument made by the Minister of Justice when he was sitting over here, yet there has been no change in three years?

I was not going to raise that point. I was going to approach it on the basis of what I think they should be doing now irrespective of what they did or what they said before. I try to carry everything on a very high plane. Mr. Chairman, I think that is just common, ordinary day to day justice, and I do hope the minister will consider altering her attitude on this matter.
There is one other item I would like to bring up at this point, and that is that I hope the minister will give us an explanation of the basis upon which she decides who can and who cannot come into this country as a landed immigrant. I have particular reference here to people who come from countries where their skin may be of a different colour to our own. I know, and it has already been stated by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, that the immigration policy of Canada is supposed not to discriminate because of race or colour. That sounds pretty good, but I want to say that as far as the policies followed in Canada are concerned, whether you want to admit it or not Canada does follow an immigration policy of discrimination because of race or colour.
Mr. Chairman, this is proved by the fact that we have for some countries what is known as a quota system. A quota system is discriminatory, whether you want to call it that or not. I would like to know on what basis quotas are set and how you decide the numbers to be admitted as between one country and another. But in particular I would like to have an explanation of the quota system as it applies to the countries of the commonwealth.
I thought that in this commonwealth we were proud of and boasted about the fact
9, 1960
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration that we were all partners in a common commonwealth, that there was no differentiation between the countries of the commonwealth because of race or colour. Yet the policy of Canada is one of discrimination as between members of the commonwealth because in some countries they are black and in others they are yellow; therefore they are placed on a quota system.
To me there is something fundamentally wrong with the way Canada develops an immigration policy when countries outside of the commonwealth are not put on a quota system and we allow their people to come in even though they may have been our enemies in two world wars. Nazis who fought against us are now in Canada, and they still maintain they are nazis. I know of one man I met in Toronto who boasted that he was a fighter for freedom in the last war. When I asked him what side he fought on he told me that he fought for Hitler. Yet we allow those people in because they are white; there is no quota.
Why is it that people from countries outside of the commonwealth, countries which were our enemies, come in free of quota, but inside the British commonwealth a quota system is established with regard to countries whose citizens are either black or yellow? I think that is wrong. It is so wrong in my estimation that I think it makes mockery of a great many of the high sounding statements and principles about which we hear so often from the Conservatives. I say that it breaks down commonwealth countries as far as our immigration policy is concerned into a series of classes, and I do not think we should break down the commonwealth into a series of classes because of differences in race or colour. This principle makes a mockery of the commonwealth, and I do not like to see that being done.
I can say very definitely that last year when I had the opportunity of attending the commonwealth parliamentary conference in Australia, where I met representatives from the commonwealth parliaments, I found they had only one criticism of Canada, and that was why we discriminated against other parts of the commonwealth through the medium of the quota system. I sincerely hope that during the course of the discussion of these estimates these points I have raised, namely the form of advertising in telling people to come here when there are no opportunities available, not making full investigations as to whether statements made against people are correct, and this matter of quotas will be fully explained by the minister.

Mr. Chairman, it is my intention to make two suggestions to the minister
4720	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration regarding possible changes in the immigration regulations so far as they affect Chinese. However, in making these suggestions I, as the first representative in this house of Chinese descent, am saddened by the fact that my task has been made difficult by some members of the Chinese community who, through their activities have brought all Chinese communities under a cloud of suspicion. The government cannot be blamed for these investigations into alleged irregularities in Chinese immigration, but rather the blame must lie on those who have sought to prey on the very understandable desire of those who wish to join members of their families in Canada.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate says that he agrees immigration is a privilege, and that is a sound principle. However, many people believe that immigration is not a right but a privilege extended to a national of a foreign country, and that it cannot be demanded as of right by that foreign national except in certain circumstances as defined by the government of the country into which the immigrant seeks admission. Whether these defined circumstances that have been laid down by the government of Canada are too narrow is another matter. If they are they can always be changed, but until that event the law must be administered as it is now laid down.
The members of the Chinese community recognize that within their midst there may be some who have contravened the law. The members of the Chinese community as a whole would be the first and indeed are the first to agree that such offenders should be dealt with by the law if they have in fact been found guilty. But because of the figures that have been published in the press regarding the large numbers of alleged illegal entries, many Chinese feel that all the Chinese community are under a cloud of suspicion.
I know the minister has stated that her department will deal with the problem in a humanitarian manner, and the Prime Minister has also stated in this chamber that the great majority of Chinese in Canada are held in respect; but in view of the conflicting figures repeated in the press concerning the number of alleged illegal entries I agree with the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that the interview given by the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police was perhaps ill-advised. I would therefore suggest to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and also to the Minister of Justice that no further press interviews be granted by the R.C.M.P. until the investigations have been completed. Certainly no one would wish to see a witch hunt in that sector of the community which has always


been regarded as law-abiding, and I am sure the innate sense of fair play which all Canadians have will not allow the reputation of the Chinese community to suffer.
I have made representations regarding these investigations to the minister on behalf of the Chinese benevolent association in Vancouver, but I would be grateful if the minister could advise later on whether she has received similar representations from the association and what reply she has made to them.
I may be impertinent in doing so, but to the Chinese themselves I extend the facilities of my office, such as they are, to those who wish to regularize their entry. I understand and appreciate that for many there are barriers such as language and fear which would make them either unable or unwilling to communicate with the officials of the department. I am prepared to make representations to the minister on their behalf, and I can only hope that my personal reputation is such that it will inspire confidence in those who wish to come forward.
Hon. members can realize that I have had a very heavy responsibility in so far as Chinese immigration is concerned, being the only representative of Chinese extraction in this house. It would be very easy for me to speak out loudly on the discriminatory aspects of Chinese immigration regulations but I have not done so, Mr. Chairman, because I wanted to establish myself as a parliamentarian rather than as a person whose usefulness was restricted to speaking on minority rights alone. I wanted to study the problem so that when I did speak I would be listened to as a person who had demonstrated that he could look at a problem along broad lines.
While hon. members will recall that I spoke on this subject of Chinese immigration in my maiden speech in 1957, hon. gentlemen will also recall that I was sued for libel by Weldon Chan because of a letter I had written in reply to a woman in West Vancouver. For the record I wish to relate the circumstances of that case, because the case against me was only dismissed comparatively recently and until it was disposed of by the courts I could not make any statement about it. Briefly the facts were as follows. On December 3, 1959 I received a four-page letter from a woman by the name of Miss Alex Toppin of West Vancouver. I do not know this woman and to the best of my knowledge I have never met her. Her letter reads as follows:
2246 Bellevue Avenue West, Vancouver, B.C.,
2 December, 1959.
Dear Mr. Jung:
I have just come home from St. Paul's hospital where I have been visiting Mrs. Chan, wife of

the man whom the immigration authorities are trying to deport from this country.
This whole affair is really disgraceful and I am writing to you to try and do something to help them. As a British subject I believe in justice for peoples of all nationalities. If Chan is caught and deported there will be adverse comment on Canada throughout the entire civilized world. This is the international refugee year. This man is an admirable citizen for any country to have. He has done nothing radically wrong, and to send a British subject back to overcrowded Hong Kong is really bordering on the fringe of lunacy and an absolute travesty of British traditions of justice and fair play. Canada is a British flag country and I feel that every thinking person should protest in the strongest possible terms about what is happening to these people.
Mrs. Chan is a slight, anxious young woman, a most pathetic figure. I have today seen Harry Fan the lawyer who is representing them and he tells me Mrs. Chan is going to Ottawa on Sunday. I hope that the minister will look into this case again.
There are basic human rights at stake here and I think that the minister should remember in the sight of God all men are equal and that the colour of our skins or our racial origins are a mere accident of birth over which we have no personal control. I am not personally Chinese but Irish, and we do not like to see our fellow human beings subjected to indignities for no proper reason.
I am a member of the Vancouver civic unity association. I understand that the association have already sent you a letter about the Chans, but have had no reply and I know that the human rights people are also interested in the case.
If all else fails I am going to write to Her Majesty the Queen. My father has the honour of being on the royal household staff in his capacity as the Norroy and Ulster king of arms and I know that Her Majesty would intervene if the position were made clear to her. It is quite usual at home to bring these kind of things to her notice.
Awaiting your reply,
Sincerely,

My reply to Miss Toppin was contained in the following letter:
Ottawa, Ont.
December 4, 1959.
Miss A. Toppin 2246 Bellevue Ave.,
West Vancouver, B.C.
Re: Weldon Chan.
Dear Miss Toppin,
I acknowledge your letter of December 2 with reference to Mrs. Chan.
I have received representations from other sources who are interested in this case, and I have made inquiries from the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. I am not at all happy with the results of my investigation. In the first place, I do not think that a husband should desert his wife and family. Whatever merit he had to his case would have vanished in my mind because his action indicates that he is not capable of accepting his basic marital obligations. If he is capable of treating his family in such a way, what can we expect from him as a Canadian citizen? Does he treat all his duties and obligations so lightly?
I am of Chinese ancestry, as you know, but in matters of this kind, I think as a Canadian. We do not want a recurrence of the George Hanna case. I have made representations to the minister of previous cases which in my opinion had merit.
However, until Mr. Chan reappears I cannot truthfully say that I have had the chance to discuss his case thoroughly. I deeply appreciate your interest, but in view of my own investigations, I must be satisfied that Chan is prepared to accept responsibility. In the meantime, I shall be pleased to convey your views to the minister.
Yours sincerely,
Douglas Jung, M.P.,
Vancouver Centre.
On the basis of what I said in that letter Chan instituted the libel action against me. It should be remembered that in the early part of November, 1959 Chan disappeared prior to the day on which he was to be deported. Subsequent to his disappearance press reports stated that his wife had no idea where he was; that she had been dismissed from her job; that she was without financial support, and that she was relying on friends. In view of these press reports and the information which I had received from the department I felt that my letter expressed my opinions in a firm but courteous way. I could easily have avoided all this unpleasantness by simply not answering Miss Toppin's letter, but as a member of parliament I felt I had a duty to reply to her inquiry; and when I learned through the press that legal action was being taken against me I felt so strongly about this case that even before departing for Vancouver I telephoned my solicitors there instructing them to accept service of the writ so this case could be heard at the earliest possible time. I felt that an important principle was involved, namely the right of a member of parliament to express his views. I hope I have succeeded in dispelling any suggestion that I was deliberately going out of my way to hurt Chan. I did not deliberately write an unsolicited letter to someone I did not even know regarding Chan. Chan had been ordered deported and had gone into hiding long before I received the letter, and I had nothing whatsoever to do with the order for his deportation.
Having established that I am not afraid to speak out against one of my own race when in my opinion such words are necessary, I think I am in a better position to make an appeal on behalf of those naturalized Chinese who are still separated from their families. Hon. members will recall that in 1957, when I spoke on Chinese immigration, my theme was the reunification of the family. That theme remains unchanged. I urge that Chinese dependants regardless of age be allowed to join their relatives in Canada. Bearing in mind Chinese customs and traditions in the family, the class of dependants should be sufficiently broad to cover not only nephews and nieces but also grandchildren where the

I believe we have a moral obligation to those early Chinese immigrants who sacrificed so much and received so little to become reunited with their families. Let us remember that those early immigrants had to pay a head tax ranging from $50 to $500 in order to come to Canada, and then they were not allowed to bring their wives or families until after 1948, when the citizenship act was amended so that these old-timers could be naturalized. For over half a century many of these early Chinese settlers were denied a normal family life, and it is a source of wonder to me that in spite of these handicaps they were able to build up a reputation as law-abiding and hard-working people.
The Chinese population in Canada amounts to approximately 50,000 out of a total of 17,500,000. When this country can bring in some 37,000 Hungarian refugees in two years, as compared with the 50,000 Chinese in Canada, it can easily be seen that if all the families were united with their dependants the total of Chinese in Canada would still be small. I realize that the working out of some of the details would present problems, but I suggest that the principle of reunited families is a sound and humane principle.
Concurrent with the reunification of Chinese families there should be a quota system set up for those who have special skills and who do not have relatives in Canada. I suggest a quota system because in my view once families had been reunited the number of * Chinese wanting to come to Canada would taper off. It is highly unlikely that an unskilled Chinese person without a family here would be in a position to come to this country, because without relatives to sponsor and care for him he would have neither the means nor the desire to come to a strange land. However, skilled persons such as doctors, nurses and technicians are in a different position. Even without relatives or sponsors these people would be able to look after themselves and would constitute a definite asset to the community.
Finally, I again urge all Canadians not to allow the current investigation into alleged Chinese immigration irregularities to distort or prejudice the status of the Chinese communities in Canada. Much of the irregularity in Chinese immigration has sprung from the desire to rejoin loved ones. I know this government appreciates this fact, and for that reason the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has stated that the innocent will not suffer. That being so, I can only hope


that those who wish to do so will take the opportunity of regularizing their entry as soon as possible.	.

I do not think that in my capacity as a member of the government I could overlook a plea such as was made to me not just by one person but by several people; and, I might say, in several cases their case was substantiated by documents. No official figure of the number involved has been given by my department, and I do not believe one has been given in the Department of Justice. Speculation has, of course, been rife, and some of the figures which have been quoted in the press arose, I think, as much from the speculation of persons outside Canada as of those living in this country. Mr. Chairman, I have taken the advice of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and have prepared a short statement which I think will probably make the position completely clear. Accordingly, I should like to state that it is not the intention in connection with the current investigation to prosecute or deport from the country any Chinese presently in Canada who have not themselves engaged in assisting other Chinese, apart from their own relatives, to enter Canada illegally.

In answer to the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate, I may say that this applies to Chinese who have themselves entered Canada illegally on the basis of having given incorrect information as to their true identity, age, marital status, relatives and similar facts relating to their family status.
Having said that I should, of course, add that these people can only be helped to establish the true facts on which to regularize their status in Canada if they come forward on their own initiative and give the department correct information about themselves. If this is not done, then the individuals concerned will always be left in a state of uncertainty and insecurity, because nothing I can say as minister can give them the complete assurance they require and need unless and until they come forward and actually establish themselves, on the basis of the correct facts, as properly landed immigrants in Canada.
I should like to say, Mr. Chairman, that I think the hon. lady has been very wise in making this statement.

I have a few observations to make, and I hope to be able to advance some suggestions which may receive the consideration of the minister.
Scarcely a month has gone by since citizenship week was observed in most communities across Canada. City councils, chambers of commerce, school authorities and other voluntary organizations such as the I.O.D.E. sponsor such observances. It is one of those occasions when Canadians are or should be reminded of their privileges, their duties and their rights. The principal privilege is the right to vote at an election of representatives to public bodies, such as municipal councils, provincial and federal parliaments. In essence it is the Canadian concept of democracy.
At one of the lakehead secondary schools during the ceremonies marking citizenship week, a letter from the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration was read to the assembly from which I wish to quote a couple of paragraphs. The minister said in her letter as follows:
Our country has been built up by men and women of many races and creeds. As we study the history of Canada we learn of the contributions which these people have made, how they tilled the land, established industries and became good citizens and neighbours.
The minister went on to say that many different nationalities were represented in the schools and that she was especially pleased to learn of the sincere comradeship that existed among students. Then she concluded with these words:
That is good citizenship and a fine introduction to the adult world in which these students will soon be taking their places.

No one here will find disagreement with those sentiments so well expressed by the minister. However, in our citizenship act there are some features which should receive the attention of the government, one of which is the problem of elderly immigrants unable to qualify for Canadian citizenship because they cannot speak English well enough.
As everyone knows, from time to time there appear before the courts for examination applicants for Canadian citizenship who, because of advanced age or because, since their arrival in Canada, they have lived in remote areas often lacking the facilities which are available in urban communities, have been unable to master an adequate knowledge of English and therefore cannot meet the requirements of the act, so the presiding judge simply turns them down. It is rather regrettable that during this session no change in the citizenship act is being considered which would recognize the need for a modification of the regulations governing the examination of prospective citizens who have lived in Canada for, say, ten years.
I know, Mr. Chairman, that a person who has resided in Canada for a period of 20 years is not required by the act to possess an adequate knowledge of the English or French language. I presume that years ago parliament recognized the difficulty of certain immigrants in being unable to learn the language, and for that reason the language requirement was not applied. I am sure the minister appreciates the predicament of a considerable number of elderly immigrants who are today prevented from obtaining citizenship because of this aspect of the law.
I have in mind several cases in my own constituency. As an illustration I wish to point to the specific example of a 79-year old lady who came to Canada from one of the Scandinavian countries quite a few years ago. She is living with a son and daughter-in-law who are both in possession of citizenship certificates. Mr. Chairman, I wish only a few minutes of the committee's time on these estimates, but first I think it would be unfair if I did not offer a word of praise for the minister who I believe is doing a tremendous job in her department. However, there are certain anomalies in the Immigration Act, and in this connection I would like to put a few observations on record this afternoon.
First, it may be advisable to draw a distinction between immigration from the free countries of the world and that from the countries behind the iron curtain. Whereas immigration from the free countries is almost exclusively with economic betterment in view-and this applies to sponsored relatives to a degree-immigration from behind the iron curtain countries as well as from China and Japan is governed substantially by sentimental reasons and the desire of relatives in free, democratic Canada to come to the assistance of their kin living behind the iron curtain. The east Europeans also regard first cousins as close relatives, and often refer to them as brothers and sisters and not as cousins.
I suggest, sir, that it is therefore advisable to broaden somewhat the regulations governing the admission of relatives from behind the iron curtain and China and Japan. It would create, I am sure, a feeling of gratitude on the part of many ethnic groups in Canada. This step would be regarded as a humane gesture on the part of the Canadian government, and I do not believe it would greatly influence the over-all immigration quotas, as the number of persons permitted to leave the countries from behind the iron curtain would still be very small, due mainly to stringent restrictions placed on those people in those countries who wish to emigrate to Canada.
I would like to suggest a few reasonable changes in the Immigration Act; first, to include first cousins in the category of close relatives; second, to extend admission permits to the nephews and nieces of Canadian citizens even if they are not full orphans, and to raise the age limit to 21 years from 18 as is now stipulated in the regulations; third, to raise the age limit of the unmarried children of brothers and sisters emigrating to Canada from 18 to 21 years of age, thus
