During the first four months of 1960 there arrived in Canada, 2,760 persons from Germany, 6,424 from Italy, 5,722 from the United Kingdom, 1,483 from Greece, etc. Those persons who apply for the admission of relatives from behind the iron curtain are in most cases old established immigrants.
Immigration from these countries not including the displaced persons, stopped almost completely in 1939. In ever so many cases the immigrants of that day are without close relatives in Canada. Many of these now have ample means to guarantee support. I suggest, sir, that if these sponsors can satisfy the Canadian authorities in this regard, and if the persons who apply for admission comply with governing immigration regulations, there should be provision made to allow these people to enter Canada.
It is a generally known fact that many who wish to join their families in Canada and apply from Poland are of non-Polish origin. For security reasons, afraid of being sent to various Soviet republics by the Communist authorities, they pose as Poles but they include thousands of Ukrainians, Jews, Lithuanians, Byelorussians and others who could be included in the immigration from Poland. This last mentioned fact can be confirmed by the respective ethnic organizations in Canada.
I urge the minister to give serious consideration to these recommendations so as to correct the anomalies in the present act and assist in easing the situation.

Mr. Chairman, I have just a few words I should like to add to the discussion that has taken place on the estimates of the
4728	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. I listened with much interest to the remarks that were made by my friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, and also to the remarks that were made by the first spokesman for the C.C.F. party, the hon. member for Vancouver East.
I have always been at a loss to comprehend what really was in the mind of the late Mackenzie King when he laid down the basic character principle to which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate referred with a large measure of support and approval. Whether it be a fair interpretation of the late hon. gentleman's words, the principle is none the less construed as meaning that the immigration policy of this country should be such as to control the immigration to Canada in a way that would overt the possibility of too large a proportion of the population belonging to races that are neither Anglo-Saxon nor French.
It seems to me that if that is a true construction of what is meant by the basic character rule it ignores a very important fact. That fact is that today in Canada about 28 per cent of our population is neither Anglo-Saxon nor French. If the basic character principle is as I have attempted to enunciate it, it strikes me that regard must be had to that very large percentage of the population that falls into racial groups which, as I say, are neither Anglo-Saxon nor French.
If the basic character principle of the late Mr. King is a principle of strict application, surely as long as we have large numbers of individuals who are desirous of coming to Canada from the countries of central and eastern Europe we should not shut the doors to desirable persons from those countries while the English, the Irish and the Scotch wait to make up their minds.
I listened attentively to the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East, who enunciated what I suppose can be fairly described as a policy of restricted immigration. That appears to be good C.C.F. philosophy. It also appears to be good Canadian Labour Congress philosophy. I suppose that in view of the new but as yet unnamed partnership between the C.C.F. party and the Canadian Labour Congress it is not surprising that the hon. member should give voice to sentiments such as those he expressed during the course of his remarks today. An immigration policy as restricted as would be the policy advocated by the hon. member and by the congress would, in my opinion, as I have stated on previous occasions in this house, be an unrealistic policy and one lacking in farsightedness.


The hon. member for Vancouver East obviously belongs to that group of individuals who suppose that immigration aggravates conditions of unemployment. The hon. member for Fort William discussed that topic a few minutes ago, and both he and I spoke on the same subject on the occasion of the debate on the address earlier this session. As the hon. member and I then pointed out, the opposite is in fact true. I think if one examines the percentage of Canadians who are unemployed in the various provinces, one will find that unfortunately those provinces which have attracted the smallest number of immigrants suffer today from the largest percentage of unemployed. On the other hand, if one examines the figures for Ontario one finds that whereas since the last war Ontario has absorbed 50 per cent of the immigrants who have come to Canada, this province has the lowest percentage of unemployed.
I was particularly sorry to hear the hon. member for Vancouver East give voice to what I call the old nazi bogey. I think I know the hon. member well enough to know that he did not intend to smear the German immigrant population of Canada, but the clear impression which would emerge from his remarks-an impression which I hope and feel sure he did not intend-is that the majority of the German immigrants to Canada are either nazis, former nazis, or nazi sympathizers. It is my experience, and I am sure it is the experience of all my colleagues who represent constituencies part of whose population consists of German immigrants, that nothing could be further from the truth. In a long association with many immigrants who have come to Canada from Germany I have found them to entertain the same feelings of revulsion that are entertained by any of us when we contemplate the terrors and the horrors of the Hitler regime.
The hon. member is not alone in the impression he created. On the same theme I have in mind the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It has been brought to my attention, in connection with the point I am now making, that the C.B.C. has seen fit in the last year or less to resurrect for its late night movies some of the old nazi horror pictures. This accomplishes nothing in the field of entertainment for fellow Canadians, but it has served to keep in mind the kind of prejudice that ought to be done away with. We have taken steps to invite people from Germany to come to this country to make it their home. Many people have come in response to that invitation and it is unfair, I would think, for a government owned institution such as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to be

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration in Canada. In that respect I think a tribute also should be paid to the editors and publishers of the foreign language newspapers of Canada, which are now published in such large numbers and have such a wide circulation among this ever-growing and increasingly important part of our population.
Those, Mr. Chairman, are some of the sentiments that I wanted to take advantage of this opportunity to express.

Mr. Chairman, I hope the hon. gentleman will permit me to say a word. I did not like to interrupt the hon. member for Parkdale but I do have to take some exception to something he said, though I am sure he said it quite innocently. He suggested that in my speech this morning I had said something about the basic character of the population referred to in Mr. Mackenzie King's statement. I said nothing about it at all. I did not even mention that particular aspect at all. I was referring to another matter entirely, the control by Canada of its own immigration policy.
I should not like it to be thought that the hon. member's interpretation of Mr. Mackenzie King's mind was one with which I agree. I always understood that what was meant was that, having developed a certain kind of Canadian outlook, we wanted to add to our population people who would contribute to that in much the way, with which I have no quarrel, that the hon. member has suggested is being done; and I would say that the best interpretation of what Mr. Mackenzie King meant is the immigration policy that was followed by the Liberal government between 1947 and 1957. But there is an authoritative interpretation to which I might direct the hon. member's attention. It was given in the house by the hon. member for Eglinton when he was sitting on this side of the house. As this is the latest authoritative interpretation of Mr. Mackenzie King's mind, and as it comes from one of the leaders of the hon. member's party, I thought he might like to be reminded of it. It is to be found on page 1196 of Hansard for February 15, 1955, at which time the hon. member for Eglinton said:
Let us face frankly the fears which immigration has engendered in some Canadians. Those fears have been principally on the grounds of race and employment. On the subject of race I think the government owes a duty-
This is the hon. member for Eglinton, the present Minister of Finance, speaking.
-to the people of Canada to say, as we Conservatives say and say emphatically, that immigration into this country must never be permitted to have for its purpose disturbance of the fundamental racial composition of Canada. We subscribe most emphatically to that point of view.


That is the hon. member for Eglinton, now the Minister of Finance.
There are those in this country who have feared immigration because they thought it offered a threat of assimilation into an English speaking community. That is not our view of immigration. We would resist with all the power at our command as a party any attempt to use immigration for that purpose. We owe a duty to Canada to allay that fear that admittedly has existed in certain quarters. I say at the same time that the government owes it to the people of Canada to make a similar declaration to allay those fears.
I think that can be regarded as the official Conservative canon on this subject, and I commend it to the hon. member for Parkdale.

Mr. Chairman, I was of course pleased to hear the minister repeat what I should like to term her credo for an immigration policy for Canada. This is not the first time she has spoken so forcefully and effectively about the necessity and desirability of increasing the population of Canada. She has made these speeches outside the house, in various parts of the country, and they have all been well received. Similar statements have been made by the Prime Minister urging a high rate of immigration. A former leader of the opposition, Hon. George Drew, at one time spoke in the house in terms of seeking 25 million immigrants for Canada. I go along with that, as I think most Canadians do, as a desirable immigration policy for Canada.
However, I am sure the minister and the government will understand that when we say things which might sound as though we were not in complete agreement with the minister or her statements, those statements should be accepted as constructive criticism. I do not want to even term it as criticism. It is true that in all honesty and sincerity, people do not agree about methods, systems or philosophies.
I feel that there is much in the present Immigration Act that could be improved. I want to address myself to those things with a view to improving the act, in the hope that the minister's expressed wish in connection with immigration will be realized. She has said she takes the long range view, but I hope she is not wearing short range glasses. It is quite possible to have a long range view on immigration and yet, in all honesty, be a little short-sighted in implementing that long range view. These are some of the things I should like to touch upon.
I do not know whether anyone, including the minister of immigration, could today laydown for Canada a clear-cut and specific immigration policy. I consider her statement today as rather vacillating. She seemed to say yes, we want immigration, but we want immigrants of a certain kind and the act says we

want them mostly from certain places. This may be quite true, but is that a long range view? Let us see, for example, what happens. We look for immigrants, preferably from certain sections of the world because we believe they can more rapidly integrate into the Canadian way of life. Unfortunately those large waves of immigrants that we speak about are not available from these quarters.
I think the long range view, and I now address myself to the minister directly, can be helped by looking at what has happened in the past. You talk about bringing in large waves of immigrants, and you look over the applicants to judge their suitability for that long range immigration program. It is quite possible that those whom we look upon now as prospective immigrants from central Europe and other parts of the world may not be the most desirable for that program. I cannot say what the reason may be. The Immigration Act apparently does make some classification.
However, I feel that the long range view of the government and of the minister would best be served by looking at the second generation Canadians. I have sat here making a fast count, and I find there are members in this house who are not first generation Canadians. There are, either in this house or the other place, roughly between 12 and 15 hon. gentlemen who are immigrants into this country. This does not mean that they may not be first class Canadians. Let us look a little further; let -'us look at the next generation of Canadians, y I was not born in this country, and that is ^ true of other members in this house. This * does not mean to say that my children are not first class Canadians or that they will not continue to be. They have worn the king's uniform and have graduated from Canadian universities.
This is what I call a long range view. Second, third and fourth generation Canadians are all Canadians. You cannot now tell from what part of Europe they came or from what country they came, whether they came from Anglo-Saxon countries or Latin countries. Today they are Canadians, and in my judgment that is the long range view which the minister should take in looking upon people who today come knocking upon our doors saying they want to come in. We should not say they are not qualified. If there is a possibility of admitting people, let us admit them. If they are qualified, if they appear intelligent, if they are in good health, if they have good records, let us accept them.
I do not believe anyone else needs to speak about large waves of immigrants. The government is doing that, the minister is
9, 1960	4731
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration doing that, the Prime Minister is doing it and the Minister of Finance is doing it; that is an accepted fact. Unfortunately I feel that legislatively and even verbally we say we want large waves of immigrants but are we really doing the things that will get them? I feel that we are not. The hon. member for Vancouver East spoke this morning about the advertisements for tradesmen to come to Canada. We have to look at the position. Either we want immigrants or we do not want them. Let us not say we want them and then make it extremely difficult for them to come. These statements may sound very well and be very satisfying and they may meet certain situations such as the one the hon. member for Parkdale referred to, keeping a certain balance. There is no question, however, but that if we look at the position today we will have a very difficult time setting up a policy. We should be looking at the future of Canada 50 years ahead, 100 years ahead or 200 years ahead; that is the kind of long range view to take, not what will happen this year or next year. We could become despondent if we were to judge the long range program by what has happened.
I believe that in 1957, if my records are correct, approximately 282,000 people came into this country. In 1958 the number dropped to 124,000. That is a staggering figure when we think in terms of large waves of immigrants about which the minister speaks. You do not increase the population of Canada when the number of immigrants is cut in half. What is the reason for this? Have we made it difficult for them to come or have we made it easy for them to come? Have we welcomed them or have we done everything possible to keep them out?
I feel, and I have felt over the years, that there has been a tendency to keep immigrants out of the country. When an immigration official examines a prospective immigrant he does not examine him from the point of view of whether he is a desirable immigrant; of what we can find in this man that will enable us to issue a visa. No; unfortunately the reverse attitude is taken. They say we must keep him out; and upon the slightest suspicion, without even investigation, as the hon. member for Vancouver East has pointed out, that is done. It is the safe thing to say no. It is always safest to say no.
I know our immigration officials abroad and in this country extend themselves as far as they can to give a favourable decision. They are very courteous, very thoughtful and very compassionate at times. However, unfortunately the regulations tie their hands. Often they cannot say so, but we have to read
4732	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration between the lines when they say no. There appears to have been a philosophy toward immigration to keep immigrants out of Canada unless they fall into a category that would maintain the balance. I do not know what ' balance. Perhaps some things are left unsaid, and sometimes that is the better way.
If we seek immigrants for Canada, I wonder whether the minister and her senior officials will take a new look. There has been some modification in the department and perhaps new officials will take a new look. I am hopeful that perhaps the officials and the minister will now take a new look at bringing immigrants into Canada. We want them. On that score I think all hon. members of the committee are fairly well agreed. The question of these tradesmen to which I referred previously leads me to one conclusion. Approximately 50 trades are listed. Every conceivable trade, employment or profession to which you can possibly refer is listed here. Canada is looking for all these immigrants or all these types of immigrants. If that is so, is it because we are looking for people as immigrants to populate our country or are we looking for tradesmen? For example, are we short of bricklayers, cooks, domestics, dry cleaning experts and so on down the list?
We are short of good government.

My hon. friend says we are short of good government. That may come in time. I am fairly sure it will come in time.
The fact is that I do not think any hon. member in the chamber, regardless of his political allegiance, will say that we in this country are short of tradesmen of these kinds.
I wonder, Mr. Chairman, whether the hon. member would tell us what it is he is reading from.

I am reading from a photostatic copy of an advertisement which appeared in the Belfast Telegraph of December 6, 1959. If this is a program to attract immigrants to Canada, well and good. I hope it is. I am not critical of it. I rather regard it more as being an advertisement to attract people from that area to come to Canada. I do not want to say it is that certainly, because I do not know; but I doubt whether similar advertisements appeared in newspapers in other continental countries in Europe. I do not know. Perhaps the minister will enlighten me. However, I feel it was directed mostly to Belfast and other Anglo-Saxon countries, being a rather direct appeal for immigrants. I am willing to accept that explanation. It is most welcome. But if we * want immigrants, it would be interesting to know whether the minister can tell us how
[Mr. Crestohl.)

much money was spent for this advertisement and how many immigrants it actually produced.
We know that there are immigrants clamouring to come to Canada and that they are not readily admitted. I do not want to say that there are obstacles, but they have difficulties because of the existing regulations. Of course, I for one am appreciative-as is the rest of the country-of the thoughtfulness of the department and the minister in admitting a number of hard-core cases. That was certainly a compassionate and humanitarian thing for the government to do. It is in line with Canadian thinking. It is in line with Canada's showing the way in assisting humanity where such assistance is required.
Then also there are refugees. The government showed fine consideration for refugees who have come to Canada. There is a third class of immigrants who now wander over the face of the globe. They are called stateless persons. Somehow or other I do not think we have ever had a complete definition or understanding of what a stateless person is. At one point the minister was asked about stateless persons. If a stateless person is in Canada and must be deported, she was asked to what state such a stateless person could be deported. I think I asked the minister that question. The very term "stateless person" indicates that you cannot deport him to any state. The minister attempted to give some sort of answer to the effect that she would deport him to the last country in which he had been if that country would take him. It is, of course, an anomalous position and I hope the minister will, in some form, give a little bit lengthier explanation of what Canada will do with a stateless person who is about to be deported.
I should also like to say a word about the Canadian government immigration policy with respect to visitors to Canada. I think the procedure with respect to visitors lends itself to the severest form of criticism. Why should we deny people the right to visit Canada? Of course the minister explained that matter in her statement of 1958. She | said that these people come here as visitors and then decide to remain here and make application. What if they do? People come and visit Canada. They like Canada. They see Canada. They decide to try to remain in Canada. There is no crime in that course. There is no offence in it. I rather think it is a compliment to Canada when they come here to visit the country, see it, like it and then ask permission to remain here. But no; the department and the act or the regulations-I do not know which it is-make of that procedure an offence. What is said to these people is this: you came here and you

fooled us; you fooled our immigration inspectors whom you saw in Europe. You said you were coming as a tourist but you had no intention of coming as a tourist, you really had the intention of remaining in Canada; and because you fooled us, we cannot consider your application.
I say that is not a generous view to take. Technically speaking the department may be right but it is not a generous approach to take. I know of a number of cases of young men who have come to this country as tourists, one to visit a brother. They are university graduates. Then they decide to remain in Canada and they apply for permission to remain. Even though this man has a brother who is resident in Canada, the department says to him, "You cannot apply while you are in Canada", because of the minister's statement in 1958. The department says, "You leave the country; you go back where you came from and when you are there, apply there and we will process you there".
Again I say that, technically, that procedure may be correct. However, in its practical application, in the economy of the whole thing, it is basically wrong. You have the man here. Examine him. Find out whether he is a good immigrant. Find out whether he is in good health or whether he qualifies. If he does so, land him here. Why send him back thousands of miles to file his application elsewhere?
There may be reasons for a thing like that. I hope the minister will explain the reasons. It just does not make good sense. It is not good business and it is not good economics. Certainly in many instances these people are desirable immigrants and we, who seek many immigrants, lose them. That is one of the faults, among many others, upon which I should like to touch in referring to the Immigration Act in a few moments.
I should also like to say a word or two about some immigrants from the Middle East, from such places as Iraq, Lebanon and other Arab countries in which it is difficult for certain people to remain in safety. I know that the department extends itself as much as possible to show special compassionate consideration for all the dangers which surround the fives of these people and tries to help.
Unfortunately they are often handicapped, not so much by the act but by the immigration regulations. I appeal to the minister that when these cases come up she should look upon them as generously as I know she can and I ask her to encourage her officials to extend themselves as generously as possible, because it is a question of human fife. If these people are forced to return to these
9, 1960	4733
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration countries some of them will not go back because it means certain death. It is almost as bad as not wanting to go back to the countries behind the iron curtain.
I make a special appeal for these immigrants from Iraq. A number of cases I know of are now before the department. All concern very fine, intelligent, well educated people of substance who are in Canada now. They are here as tourists or students but they live under the constant fear of being asked to leave Canada. I make an appeal on their behalf. Perhaps they do not fall within the four corners of the act at the present time, but there are certainly grounds in the act which allow the minister a certain latitude to deal with these very special cases, and they deserve the department's and the government's most sympathetic attention.
I know of the case of a stateless person, for example, where I am told the department went to the embassy of the country where that person ran away from because of certain fears that person had and asked the embassy, will they take this person back? It becomes a very painful situation. It is even painful to talk about because these things are filled with tears right down the fine. I hope the department will stretch the immigration regulations as far as it possibly can to give these people the necessary relief.
I should like to deal with this question of visitors and to quote very briefly from a statement once made by the present Prime Minister when he was sitting in opposition. On January 26, 1957 he said:
Petty little legalities should not interfere with the admittance to this country of someone who is physically and mentally fit.
I rather admire that statement. It was a lofty statement for the Prime Minister to have made at that time.
Again, he said on September 20, 1954:
Good citizens should not have their way impeded by roadblocks and departmental red tape. We have lost many excellent immigrants.
I cite these quotations not because the department is not familiar with them or because the minister does not understand them but because I feel they should go on record if for no other reason than it is another nudge in the direction of doing away with minor legal technicalities and allowing these people to emigrate to Canada.
I should now like to point out to the minister a number of anomalies, and 1 am glad her officials are in the chamber. The hon. member for Edmonton East pointed out some anomalies contained in the act and the regulations and I would like to point out some which are really very painful. There are five subsections to section 20 of the act dealing with regulations applying to immigrants.
4734	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Under subsection (a) immigrants from some countries need nothing else to enter Canada except some means to maintain themselves until they find a job. That is the only requirement they need; to be in good health, of good morals and have a little money to keep body and soul together until they get a job. That is very admirable and to be commended. However, in another subsection we find that from other countries immigrants need nothing else except to come to a job which is already waiting for them or to establish themselves in business, in a trade or profession or in agriculture. Again, as in the previous case, the question of having close relatives in Canada does not enter into it. If a man can comply with these items he becomes admissible. I commend that section. It is a fine section. That does not make immigration into Canada difficult, but proper as it should be.
There is another subsection which lists certain countries and only the close relatives enunciated in the section are admissible. In this category there are no limits provided the immigrant is in good health and is a relative as defined. The question of occupa-1 tion does not enter into it. A potential immigrant may have means and a job, but if he does not have close relatives as defined he will not be admitted. To my way of thinking that is contradictory.
A further subsection refers to other countries and lists the same close relatives as in the previous subsection except that the parents of a Canadian citizen in this case must be over a certain age, 65 years in the case of the father and 60 years in the case of the mother. I have spoken about this before. I find it extremely difficult to understand the reasoning behind this subsection. I do not see how anyone in good sense can say that is a desirable regulation. If the father is 64 years of age he cannot be admitted; he must be 65 or over. Surely hon. members will not deny that a father of age 64 is just as beloved to his child as is a father of 65 or 66. Why should one not be allowed to bring his father to this country even if he is only age 64? The same applies to a mother. If the mother is 59 years of age she is not admissible-I am speaking now of the mothers of Canadians-if she is 60 or 61 she is admissible. How can one possibly draw such a fine line? I wonder who the genius is that set down those fine lines of demarcation?
I can answer that question, Mr. Chairman. It was the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.

I was just on the point of saying that. If that genius was a member of the former government I assure the hon. gentleman can accept that criticism in a lofty


sense. Is the minister now saying to me that that was a good regulation enacted by the former minister? If so, let the hon. lady get up and say so.

speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps you might allow me to reply to the hon. member for Cartier and then he could proceed. As the hon. lady has said, I was responsible for the drafting of that particular regulation. I think perhaps the hon. member for Cartier would like to know why it was drafted that way. It was done that way because these categories apply to countries that are under communist domination and, I think, only to those countries. It was on the advice of the security officers that it was done that way. Since we could do no security clearance in those countries at all and there were no facilities of any kind for that it was the view of the advisers of the government, which in this case I accepted, that the risk of a man over 65 or a woman over 60 or of children ' of the ages specified was a risk that we could very reasonably take.
I may say I have no doubt that the hon. lady does just what I did when there was some case of great merit where the father was 64. We asked the governor in council to be generous in the matter. I admit at once that the hon. member was correct in saying that on the surface this looks completely silly. I simply wish that we lived in the kind of world where we did not have to have any kind of security screening at all because it is the most unpleasant and objectionable thing about immigration and, I think, about every other aspect of our lives in a world that considers itself civilized.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The procedure, of course, has been for the Chair to recognize an hon. member from the other side of the house. I recognize the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard.

Mr. Chairman, I wish I had had the opportunity of rising a few moments ago when we had an hon. lady of this house occupying the Chair because I think it was an historic occasion to have an hon. lady chairman when an hon. lady minister's estimates were under review.
I wish it was my lot today to pay tribute to the minister for all the wonderful things that her department has done but I should like to restrict my comments at this time to one facet of the Immigration Act and that is the procedural part of the legislation.
Many statements have been made inside and outside of the chamber since 1957 to

the effect that the House of Commons in due course would be considering a new Immigration Act, an act which I believe hon. members will recognize as being one in which I have become extremely interested. To date we have had no opportunity and no assurances that we will shortly be considering this often-discussed new immigration bill. In that regard it is rather disappointing to me not to have had an opportunity to speak about it because during the election campaigns I stated to my constituents that I would fight vigorously for a new immigration bill.
I do not propose to speak at length today because I have already spoken on this subject on previous occasions here in the House of Commons and certainly on many occasions outside the house. My chief suggestion to the minister is that at the earliest possible moment we be given an opportunity of considering a new immigration bill. I believe it is now too late in this session to provide such an opportunity but I hope mention of this will be included in the throne speech at the next session.
With the advent of the revised act of 1952 many hoped that the evils, uncertainty and the rigid ministerial control which for many years had plagued the field of immigration would be mitigated. Provision was made for an immigration appeal board. Certainly that was a step in the right direction. The sections of the old act were re-arranged, additional definitions were inserted and the result appeared to be a better example of legislation. Unfortunately little of substance was altered and the act together with its regulations remain in my opinion as one of the saddest statutes on the books today. As far as many of us are concerned-those of us who practise in this field and I presume many other hon. members do-frustration, bewilderment and confusion have become the common lot of those engaged in this departmental work. The administration of the act has been carried on in a general atmosphere , of secrecy, in the main, which has certainly in the city of Vancouver, and I suggest elsewhere, provoked sharp criticism from the bench and the bar and certainly from the press.
Since world war II, mainly as a result of the efforts made by the Canadian Bar Association, ministerial discretion in various departments of government has been drastically reduced. Perhaps the best example can be found in the administration of the Income Tax Act which points to a tendency to restore the administration of public departments of government to the field of law. Both the Income Tax Act and the Unemployment Insurance Act provide excellent machinery for
9, 1960
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the hearing of grievances and of appeals and with the improvements which are being made annually in those administrative procedures few can find anything to criticize in the administration of those two government departments.
The trend has been the same in the provincial field and numerous new statutes enacted in the past decade have been careful to provide adequate machinery for the hearing and appealing of applications, ministerial orders and the like. The Immigration Act, however, remains as an outstanding exception to this general tendency.
Since world war II Canada has received approximately two million immigrants. Certainly credit is due to the previous administration for bringing so many people to this country. They have made excellent residents and citizens of this nation. It is the hope particularly in my area that the present government will pursue just as vigorous an immigration policy. If my memory serves me correctly, immigrants to Canada since the last war have brought $1J billion to this country in the way of assets. Certainly they have brought new ideas and modes of carrying on business and these contributions have been welcome.
The present Immigration Act serves the masses who come to Canada. I have no complaints about that aspect of the act but I suggest it does not serve the increasing numbers of those who run into difficulties under the act. It has been the immigrants with problems that have focussed our attention on the inadequacies of the act. I suggest it is in this field of procedural problems that we have attracted the sharpest criticism from judges and the press. Many have become aware of the shortcomings of the act and I suggest there is now a widespread call, in fact a demand, that the act be completely changed.
Certainly any student of immigration law has strong feelings about the practices and procedures of the department. It is known that I have written many letters on the subject and have had the honour to serve on a committee of the Canadian Bar Association dealing in particular with immigration procedures. Since coming to Ottawa as a member I have strongly advocated changes in the legislation because, as I have indicated to the minister and to you, Mr. Chairman, we said in my riding that we would fight for a new immigration act. Again I say how disappointing it is to me that we have not yet had a bill brought before us.
At this time I should like to commend the staff of the immigration department for the

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration job they have tried to do under a most difficult and unworkable act. They have certainly been loyal and trustworthy but I can readily see that no minister or civil servant could really do the job that is required under the present act.
I would very much like to be able to commend the provisions of the act because I believe that all concerned know it is just not my nature to publicly criticize anyone personally and indeed I find it difficult to criticize publicly even the procedural aspects of the department. In 1957 the Vancouver Sun said in an editorial:
Surely Ottawa is capable of devising a system that looks fair and humane while still protecting Canada against inflow of subversives and undesirables.
Public policy demands it, aside from the urgency of protecting Canada's reputation as a country which respects human rights ...
When an immigrant isn't satisfied with rejection by a special inquiry officer, he should have access to a fair appeal procedure.
The article went on:
To get to the courts, a would-be immigrant must claim that immigration department proceedings were so unfairly or so badly conducted as to violate natural justice. This is a shocking accusation to have made-and upheld by the courts- against the Canadian government several times a year.
That is the objective toward which I am trying to work today. We should try to bring about a system that will not attract such sharp criticism. Recently one of the learned judges of the supreme court of British Columbia said that those who had knowledge of the act were not working hard enough to bring about changes in it. He said at that time that he was adding his voice, as a voice in the wilderness, in an effort to bring about changes.
We are disturbed at the present time about the Chinese problem in many parts of Canada, but before we become too critical of that minority group, should we not consider the system under which they enter this country? Hon. members may look as long as they please, but they will find no rules, no regulations, no section of the act, setting out the procedures under which these people enter. There is a marked shortage of regulations guiding their admission, and I suggest that those Canadians who are applying for dependants are entitled to better treatment in this respect. Surely we could devise a system under which they could enter, clearly knowing what was being done. Some rules should be established with respect to the hearing overseas, and others to govern appeals in cases in which applications are rejected.
All too frequently one hears the argument that these matters are not very serious, that

only a small minority group is affected. The applicants are, nevertheless, Canadian citizens and the words used by Mr. Justice Duff, as he was then, in a well-known case known as Samejima versus The King which is to be found in the library referring to a deportation order 23 years ago, still apply as ever. He said:
I gravely fear that too often the fact that these enactments are, in practice, most frequently brought to bear upon orientals of a certain class, has led to the generation of an atmosphere which has obscured their true effect. They are, it is needless to say, equally applicable to Scotsmen. I admit I am horrified at the thought that the personal liberty of a British subject should be exposed to the hugger mugger which, under the name of legal proceedings, is exemplified by some of the records that have incidentally been brought to our attention.
I agree that the oriental situation is in many ways the most serious immigration question we face at the present time. Persons claiming Canadian citizenship over the years have been barred from Canada. Intending immigrants and relatives of Canadian citizens have been rejected on a visual estimate of age corroborated by a pseudo-scientific radiological procedure. I agree that a decision is difficult in cases of this kind, but I say that if we grant a hearing overseas it should be a fair hearing. I suggest that at present it is not a fair one and that we should correct the situation and bring about at an early date a procedure whereby a copy of the transcript relating to the hearing overseas is made available to the Canadian applicant. Certainly, over the years, persons have been granted admission by order in council, but at a later time a visa has been refused. There has been a lack of any form of hearing. There has been a refusal to allow counsel to be present at these overseas hearings, a position which has attracted sharp criticism.
Another editorial which apeared in the Vancouver Province had this to say:
An intending immigrant, once refused admission may butt his head against the stone walls of the department as long as he likes without learning the real reason he was denied admission.
It is with situations of this sort that I rise today to deal. It is my desire to persuade the minister and her officials, if I can, to devise some rules which will give these people a chance. This does not necessarily mean that we will have to amend the act, because many of these questions are procedural matters which could be corrected by order in council. Many problems are involved, and I know it is impossible to please everyone, but I say we should not hesitate to condemn a policy, carried out on a basis of secrecy, which refuses to give reasons for the actions it takes

and which does not provide a proper tribunal so that a full and fair hearing is given to the Canadian dependents.
In considering the new act I hope the minister will consider establishing a quota system for Canada so that Canada can receive from all countries, including those in the British Commonwealth, some immigrants from each country. A quota system would in the main be a new departure although we have a quota system in effect already respecting the East Indian community. A quota ' system could, to a large degree, follow the system used in the United States and it would result in many people who are not at present admissible becoming eligible for admission to Canada.
I should like, also, to see easier entry made possible for persons who are able to support themselves. There are many people who would like to live here almost indefinitely, without necessarily taking employment here. I am thinking, for example, of writers and artists. There may be other classes of people in this position, including elderly people who would like to reside here; people who have ample means and who, again, would like to settle here indefinitely. Under the regulations as they are at the moment hon. members will find that many industrialists, importers and exporters are barred from Canada unless they have a son, or a daughter or a wife in this country.
In making these suggestions I should like the minister to consider the following proposals. First, that the departmental regulations be codified and that departmental practices relating to the application or interpretation of the act be supplied to all persons interested. A statement of policy by the minister has in the past been relied upon as the basis of admission or rejection of applicants. In the past statements have been made in the house which formed the basis and the only basis upon which some dependents of Canadians could enter the country. I suggest that that is something we should overcome and that the regulations in that regard should be codified.
The second point is that certified copies of all applications and all exhibits and other material upon which decisions are based should be supplied at a reasonable cost where it is established that the document is not available to the applicant.
Third, the procedure in dealing with applications for admission and for other matters dealt with at immigration stations should follow a standard pattern. Those of us who have had experience with the department find that the same procedure is not followed
9, 1960	4737
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration at the various ports of entry. It is for that reason I am making that suggestion at this time.
Next, there should be an appeal to the courts on all matters of interpretation of law and on all other grounds recognized as proper grounds for appeal from administrative tribunals.
Next, I say that all statements made at any investigation, inquiry or examination-in making this suggestion I have in mind that we are dealing with dependants of Canadians, not necessarily immigrants from overseas who have no close relatives in Canada-relating to the applicant's status or that of his dependants should be under oath and be in writing or be reduced to writing and that the applicant should be given a copy of part or all of the transcript subject to the payment of a reasonable fee.
Next, I suggest that an immigration appeal board, as provided in the act, be established and that it hear not only appeals from deportation orders but also from the refusal of a visa, again where dependants of Canadians are involved. I suggest that the appeal board should have jurisdiction to determine questions of both law and fact, and that the right of the minister to decide which appeals shall and which shall not go to the board should be deleted. In other words, the suggestion here is that in each and every case these appeals should go to the board and that the minister should have no right to delegate these cases to herself in some instances.
The next suggestion is that written reasons should be furnished by the minister or by the board for the rejection of appeals. This would be most helpful to members of the house and to the many Canadians who are interested in immigration problems.
Next, I suggest the formulation of a policy of bail under section 18 which would confer discretion on a special inquiry officer. The present policy is dictated by the department and it does not allow security by the depositing of title deeds to real property and the like. I would particularly ask the minister to deal with this aspect of the problem when she is commenting later because many people arrive at the Vancouver port of entry after five o'clock at night and it is my understanding that there is no provision even for accepting a cash bond at that time and that on the following day a cash bond is specifically requested. The department cannot accept the security of title deeds and so on, which would be of help to those who wish to assist in arranging the bond. Surely an applicant should not be at any greater disadvantage
4738	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration than he would be if he were involved in a matter before a criminal court.
Next, Mr. Chairman, I suggest the restoration to the immigration officer in charge at a port of entry of jurisdiction to hear and determine applications under section 20 (2) of the regulations. In this regard, and I again mention this by way of constructive criticism, at the port of Vancouver, for example, we have long felt that this authority has been moved 3,000 miles to the west. When persons, particularly dependants of Canadians, now come to Vancouver they merely show a document when they get off the plane and they move in very quickly. It seems to me from reading the act that there is a duty upon the officer in charge to conduct an examination at that time. Under the present practice we have moved the port of entry, as I have suggested, many miles to the west with the result that all of these matters are handled overseas and the officer in charge has very little to do when the people arrive.
I know that problems will arise if this suggestion is followed. You may ask what we are going to do if people come over here and we have to turn them back. It may be that the solution to the problem would be to give them their medical examination overseas and then bring them in in lots of 10 by plane to Vancouver where the examination could be conducted. In the Vancouver area at least I suggest that this might be tried as an experiment. The applicant could meet the dependant, both could be put under oath and there could be a more formal hearing with the opportunity for an immediate appeal from any rejection. I say that there is great room for improvement and I think we can overcome many of the problems if we follow the suggestions I have made.
Lastly, I suggest that any person alleging Canadian citizenship should have the right, upon establishing a prima facie case, to be permitted to proceed to a port of entry, instead of being heard at a place abroad, for a hearing under section 20 of the act. Over the years there have been people who have said, "I am a Canadian" and the officer has said, "I do not think you are". Then the officer proceeds to hear the case at the overseas point. I suggest that we follow the United States system and that where a person says, "I am a Canadian"-in this day and age it is a very nice thing to be able to say- that person should be able to proceed to the port of entry. I am quite agreeable to obliging that person to remain in custody but certainly there would then be a hearing and also access to the courts afterward. I feel that is a much better system than the one we follow at present.


I also suggest that there should be an amendment to section 33 of the act which requires a deportation order to be executed as soon as practicable, to provide that the service of an application to a court attaching the order shall operate as a stay of proceedings. In the most recent celebrated case in Vancouver the deportation order has been confirmed by the court. Technically speaking, the immigration officer could immediately pick up that person and transport her out of the country. But I suggest that where a matter has been before the courts and there is a chance of appealing the department should not act further until the appeal period has expired or at least counsel should certainly be given a reasonable time in which to serve an order upon the department indicating an appeal will be taken.
There are one or two other suggestions I wish to make in connection with some of the British cases that have come to my attention. In the past we have known of cases where, for example, five members of a family out of six can meet our medical qualifications and it sometimes happens that the department will say that the five may come but the sixth must stay. I should like to say that perhaps we cannot always insist upon grade A immigrants, so to speak, but that we do the best we can to get the best immigrants in an area. If in a family there is one who cannot meet the medical qualifications, particularly if that person be under 21 years of age, then I feel we should allow the whole family to come to Canada and we should take our chances with respect to that family.
I hope, Mr. Chairman, that the minister will give early consideration to the many recommendations that have been made by the Canadian Bar Association with respect to immigration procedures. Certainly the members of that committee worked hard and long and those recommendations have been before the present administration for some three years. We hope that at an early date some of these suggestions can be incorporated into our immigration procedures. I should like to feel that at an early date, a house committee could be formed in order that we could deal with the many trouble spots in our immigration act, particularly with reference to our procedures.
I suggest to the minister also that where a Canadian employer files an application for a specific person to be his employee, that type of case should be expedited, especially where the minister is absolutely satisfied this is a bona fide application. If the application is delayed too long, let us say beyond six months, the circumstances in the place of employment might change and the

employee may no longer be needed. I would ask that some consideration be given to that type of case.
I have dealt at length with the matter of the quota system, and it is something by means of which I feel we could get many new and wonderful immigrants to Canada. For example, there may be a particular medical student in the Fiji islands who may not be admissible, there may be a medical student possessing wonderful qualifications on the island of Formosa who might be available or the president of the Hong Kong university might wish to come to Canada. When we have no quota system these people are not admissible, shall we say, as a matter of right.
In closing, may I suggest that at an early date we discontinue emphasizing that immigration is a matter of privilege and not of right. I suggest that we in Canada may need the immigrant more than the immigrant needs us. We should say to the people of Great Britain, for example, come and be a part of us; help us to build up this country. The main idea I am trying to convey here is, let us try to create a fair climate at home to encourage these people to come and make a home. I have a further suggestion and it is that we try to convey to tourists that they may proceed through customs and immigration very quickly when they come to Canada. We spend a great deal of money on advertising in the United States inviting people to come here, and we have had occasion to find that when they get to the border they run into major difficulties.

I was pointing out some of the anomalies in the present act, and I quite innocently asked the question, who is this genius who is responsible for inserting these anomalies into the act? I was interested in the alacrity with which the minister jumped to her feet and pointed her finger at the genius, the former minister of immigration.
That is the usual service.

I am glad she recognizes his ability because during the three years that she has been in office she has done nothing to correct these anomalies. I think perhaps she should accept some of the responsibility because she has acted upon these sections of the act. I was, of course, not surprised to note the frankness and honesty of the former minister, who rose without hesitation and said, "I was that genius".

I do not believe I used the word "genius".
9, 1960	4739
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration

Then give me the pleasure of using it because I think very seriously about that. The former minister did state that on reflection today the reasons that necessitated these provisions were not sociological reasons, but were security reasons. I believe that in those years security certainly was a very good reason to adopt the strictest kind of legislation, even though it now appears silly as the former minister had no hesitation in stating. I, therefore, now draw these facts to the attention of the minister, and perhaps these anomalies should be corrected.
For example, under some of these sections if the grandparents of Canadian citizens live in some countries they are admissible to Canada but if they have the misfortune to have grandparents living in another country they would not be admissible to Canada. After all, grandparents and grandchildren are human beings and should be considered as such. I think it is an anomaly to say that because the grandparents live in one country they are admissible and if they live in another country they are not admissible. I should like to ask the minister to look at these anomalies. Then there is the question of children and in this respect I have a little difficulty in considering the act as sociologically humane, if I may use that extravagant language. Children under 21 who are unmarried are admissible to Canada from some countries, but if they are over 21 they are not admissible even though they may still be unmarried. If there is a year's difference in age that clashes with the regulations. Again I point out to the minister this certainly requires a second look. If prospective immigrants to Canada have an unmarried daughter of 20 they can bring her to Canada; she is admissible. However, if that daughter should be 22, even though she may be unmarried, she is not admissible and it may be difficult for the parents to leave that child where she is in order that they may come to Canada. I think that should be looked at.
May I point out another difficult situation which can develop in the case of the parents of Canadian citizens, if the Canadian citizens want to bring their parents to this country. If the father is 64 years of age and the mother is 62, the mother is admissible because she is over 60 but the father is not admissible because he is not yet over 65. The mother can come to Canada but the father cannot. Certainly during the years when security regulations required such provisions for the protection of Canada they may have been justified, but I do not believe the danger is quite as great today.
I therefore think the time has come to examine the act in order, amongst other
4740	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration things, to correct these human touches which are really the most basic in human relations. These regulations seem to conflict with the minister's statement that it is the desire of our immigration law to bring families together, not to separate them. As they exist at present they are an ingenious means contrived to keep them apart. If we are going to blame that result on security, I respectfully submit that the danger is not quite so great now.
This brings me to the question of my wanting to make some observations on revising the act generally. Right from the commencement of this session we have been urging or trying to urge or nudge the minister into telling the house whether she plans to have the Immigration Act revised. At the beginning of the session, if I remember correctly-I have not the quotation in Hansard in front of me at the moment-the minister said that the matter of the revision of the act was receiving the attention of the department or the government, I do not remember which it was. Later on the minister made a statement in the house, as she also did outside of the house, to the effect that there will be no revision of the act at this session. We did not let the matter rest there. We pressed the matter further and on May 19 the hon. member for Trinity put this question and I am now reading from Hansard at pages 4029 and 4030:
I wish to address a question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. In the light of statements made outside this house as to the urgency of amending the Immigration Act, can the minister say whether amendments will be brought forward at this present session?
The minister replied as follows:
I have answered that question three times already this session but I am still unable to give a definite answer.
This is a rather contradictory statement when the minister says, "I have already answered the question but I cannot give a definite statement".
Read my next remark.

Yes; I will read the next remark. It was as follows:
I should probably explain that that is my Dutch blood coming out.
What a very delightful remark that was, Mr. Chairman. It is very significant. It leads me to digress for a moment from what I want to say. This is a classical example of why the minister should take what I recommended earlier, namely a long range view. I did not know that the minister was of Dutch extraction. Certainly it just confirms that long range view, that we do not look at immigrants coming in and should not look


at the first generation. But certainly I am satisfied that the minister, coming from a fine line of Dutch descent-
That is only one of them; I have several others.

The minister has several other descents or several other lines. This fact more effectively confirms my statement. Earlier I referred to the fact when I mentioned there were a number of members in the House of Commons like the minister who certainly are not native born Canadians whose ancestry goes back 200 or 300 years. I think the only ones who fall into that category would probably be the Indians. I should like to put on the record, as a matter of interest, that the following members of the House of Commons-and I am subject to correction; I may be slightly in error-certainly are today considered to be among the finest citizens in the country. They are the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, the hon. member for Fort William, the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort, the hon. member for High Park, the hon. member for Ontario, the hon. member for Marquette, the hon. member for Hamilton East, the hon. member for Mackenzie and the hon. member for Cartier. I could also name some in the other place. I respectfully say that these are all immigrants into this country. At best they may perhaps be first generation immigrants, although I doubt it. I believe those I have mentioned are not native born Canadians. Certainly no one will question or doubt that they are fine Canadians, of the finest rank and finest level. I repeat that certainly their children and their families will be Canadians almost as native, I think, as any Canadians could wish to be.
That is really taking a long range view. That is what I mean by admitting people into this country as long as they qualify. Certainly this country will have as much reason to be as proud of our immigrants who will come in to the country in the future as we have been proud of those who have come in in the past.
To come back to the subject with which I was dealing and to move away from the minister's ancestors about which I was pleased to learn, I want to talk about the question of revision. I have quoted the minister's answer about revising the act. I should now like to support this thought-and I hope the minister is giving it some serious consideration-by simply quoting from one or two newspaper editorials. First of all I should like to refer to an editorial in the Montreal Star on January 4, 1960, and I will just read a short part of it. It is entitled "Time for Overhaul". I am sure the minister and certainly the members of her staff must have

seen these editorials. However, I want them to go on record. I now quote from the one to which I have just referred:
Without delay, the Immigration Act should be reviewed and the operations of the immigration department surveyed. Either, if not both, is in need of liberalization.
Of course this word "liberalization" is spelled with a small "1". If it were spelled with a capital "L", I would not have been surprised. In my opinion it would have been just as effective, if not more so. I continue reading from the editorial:
Arbitrary behavior on the part of department personnel would lead one to think sometimes that they are constitutionally hostile to immigration. It is a question whether they should have the power of discretion they sometimes exercise.
Then there is another editorial from the same paper at a later date, namely April 27, 1960. It is entitled "Immigration Rules Need Further Change", and it reads in part as follows:
A year ago drastic changes were made in immigration regulations to permit appeal in all deportation cases. The circumstances of the Rebrin case now before a court in Vancouver suggests that the changes were not drastic enough, that it is still possible in this country to deny a person the rights which the Prime Minister is so eager to safeguard by his bill of rights.
This is not intended to be a judgment on the case of Miss Rebrin. It is intended to be a judgment on the Immigration Act and its regulations which still vest too much discretion in the minister and not enough in the law.
Then there is a third quotation I should like to read. It is from the Globe and Mail of May 24, 1960, a quite recent date. It reads in part as follows:
There is a certain attractive logic about the proposition, and if it just happened to be correct, reform of the Immigration Act would be an attractive piece of pre-election legislation. Lord knows, there are enough things wrong with the act now, with its involved procedures and arbitrary authority; the government can hardly be thinking of anything more restrictive. Therefore if it is to be made more liberal, it may have occurred to >>
someone that this will be much too effective voter bait to waste when there is no national fishing expedition in the offing.
I wonder whether there is something to this article? Perhaps the minister does plan to revise the Immigration Act. It is obvious to the house that at one time, not so long ago, she was thinking of revising the act. She said she would, but changed her mind, perhaps because it might have been a little too soon to provide the effect that this article suggests. To me it would be a matter of great indifference when the minister revises the act as long as she does revise it. It needs revision urgently and certainly the minister would be given the credit for a substantial revision of the act.
Mr. Chairman, I think one section of the act, section 39, is violently explosive in many
9, 1960	4741
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration ways. I think the minister and her officials should sometimes feel a little embarrassed by some of the language used by our courts when referring especially to section 39, which section denies any recourse to the courts. I think the minister would do the word "justice" a great deal of good and perhaps enshrine it in the manner it should be enshrined if she would allow appeals to be taken to the courts. That was a bad piece of legislation regardless of who was responsible for it. I do not hesitate to criticize legislation if I think it is bad irrespective of who enacted it. If it is bad, it is bad, and I do not hesitate to say so. But I think the minister could make a lot of corrections and improve the act considerably.
I do not want to burden the record by quoting some of the opinions of our courts, but I would feel very much embarrassed if I were the minister by some of the things our judges have said. I think it is a travesty of justice to say to Canadians, or to anyone for that matter, "You can have no recourse to the court; I, or my officials, are infallible; we don't make mistakes; our word or the decision of an inquiry officer is to be as final as a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada; we have legislated to that effect and parliament has said we have the right to do it." I do not think parliament foresaw that, and if parliament did enact it I think a wise government will bring from time to time before parliament legislation which should be corrected. It would most certainly win commendation and praise from everybody if the minister remedied those defects.
I want to conclude by appealing to the minister and her officials, as I have in the past, to treat this legislation with humanity. It is true that the law of print is cold, but I know of no other department in the government which should lend itself to sympathetic and humane understanding as much as should the department of immigration. This act and acts of a similar kind with respect to naturalization, for example, give this country the reputation of being one of the finest countries in the world, and I urge the minister to see that nothing is done with immigration legislation which might mar that wonderful reputation.

Mr. Chairman, I have heard many remarks concerning immigrants during the past year, and for that reason I wish to speak about the beneficial impact immigrants have had on the Canadian economy as expressed on different occasions by our Minister of Citizenship and Immigration who as a woman has a great understanding of our immigration policy. My remarks should
4742	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration be of great interest to many people of Waterloo North as this part of Waterloo county is one of the greatest cosmopolitan centres in Canada. We in this district well understand the fine contribution these people have made over many years and will continue to make in the future progress of Canada. I understand that this year Canada will welcome the two millionth immigrant since the end of world war II and we are interested in knowing that one out of every eleven persons in this country is now a newcomer.
I believe that the economic contribution of immigrants has three main aspects; its effects on the labour force; the building of new industry and the remanning of our farms; and the contribution of immigrants as consumers. A highly significant fact about post-war immigration is that over three quarters of the immigrant workers are in the highly productive working ages of between 20 and 44. Consequently there is a much lower proportion of immigrants among older workers.
It must be recognized that Canada's future will depend to a large extent on expansion. This in turn will depend on the new developments, some in remote areas, which occur. Development depends on people, and from this it becomes evident that many newcomers from many nations will be welcomed to Canada for all of the foreseeable future.
Opportunities for newcomers usually arise in three ways. First, the development of new jobs in an expanding economy requires skills which cannot be fully met from the domestic labour pool. For example, from 1950 to 1958, while our universities graduated 1,037 architects we admitted 1,493 more, and considering that Canada lost 330 due to emigration these professional people were of vital importance to our national growth, as were also the engineers, draftsmen, designers, teachers, accountants, scientists and others who have added so much to our professional manpower.
Mr. Chairman, I am sure that you are familiar with the shortage of teachers since the war. It is gratifying to know that in order to overcome this we were fortunate in having 6,105 teachers and professors come to Canada in the five-year period ending December 1958.
Positions also become vacant for immigrants, as native born workers are attracted to other countries. Perhaps many of us do not know that Canada lost more than 10,000 nurses to the United States from 1950 to 1958 and while we have actively sought replacements overseas, our hospitals are still desperately short.


We are hopeful that some day the tide may swing in our favour, that the time will come when Canada will attract more young Americans. In January of this year there was an encouraging sign. At last some of our universities are able to pay higher salaries and to induce not only Canadian teachers to return, but also to attract United States professors. Last year, for example, we admitted 10,350 United States citizens compared to 9,695 in 1958.
In the last two years I have had the privilege of sending almost 1,000 letters to new Canadians in my riding. These people along with others have made a great contribution to the economy of our country. They have become fine citizens and in most cases have lived up to the laws of our country. Hard work, co-operation and harmony have been the keynote of their success. Hard work overcomes financial difficulties. Co-operation enables us to work together as a team. Harmony has been a word of hope for them.
As I said before, our new Canadians have in the past and can in the future contribute much to the welfare of our great country. May I present to hon. members a few examples of the efforts of new Canadians on Canadian soil.
Mr. Leon Koerner, a Czech lumberman deprived of his holdings by Hitler, used his talents to build one of the largest companies of its kind in Canada, providing employment for 4,500 workers. Mr. Koerner soon saw that the abundant hemlock was little used by Canadians and created a brand new product, Alaska pine. By 1956 his company had many holdings. This gentleman also set up the Koerner Foundation for the promotion of art, culture and welfare. Who can measure the importance of this single immigrant to our economy?
In Vancouver three Austrian immigrants founded Canadian Forest Products Limited and built it into one of the giants of the west coast lumber industry with several divisions employing well over 1,000 people.
Thomas Bata, the Czech shoemaker, created not only an industry in Canada but also founded a new town around his plant.
For 12 years the Bick family from Holland were ordinary muck farmers near Toronto before seizing an opportunity to grow and market fresh pickles. The Bick Pickle Company during its peak last year employed 140 workers and produced a million cases of 33 different varieties.
These are but a few of the newcomers who have given much to Canada. But there are hundreds of smaller operations woven into the texture of our economy. Last year the settlement division of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration reported that it had

helped 1,750 immigrants to buy 1,612 small businesses. These provided a livelihood for 6,518 persons. This was a record year for the number of immigrants established. Some of these small businesses turn into highly profitable concerns which become important elements of the Canadian economy.
Farm settlements in 1959 were equally encouraging and showed a 16.7 per cent increase over.the previous year. Last year immigrants reported they had bought 876 farms and rented 145 more, compared with 786 farms bought and 73 rented in 1958. Half of these gave employment to others beside the operator.
Mixed farming, involving the raising of cattle in combination with the production of hogs and poultry and the growing of some cash crops, is chosen by half the immigrant farmers. Dairying is the next most popular type of farming.
Undoubtedly this thriftiness stems from the knowledge that a loss has been sustained in the sale of one's home and belongings and the move to another country. The newcomer very naturally wants to recover these material losses as quickly as possible. Also he wants to feel that he belongs to Canada.
Waterloo county, as have other counties, has been blessed with thrifty people of all nationalities enjoying freedom of religion, freedom of speech, et cetera. We cannot measure these talents, but we know that we are richer for possessing them and that they help Canada grow toward maturity. Let us give our sincere encouragement to all newcomers. They need a word of welcome which so many people of our Waterloo North have extended to them. A helping hand as we go along life's pathway together could be the difference between success or failure for them. The future lies before us, beckoning and challenging us to grasp the opportunities to build a great nation. Together, old and new Canadians, let us rise to the challenge of the soaring sixties.

If, as is apparently the situation, there are a number of people of Chinese extraction who have entered Canada through this illegal method or this racket that has existed, then this fact would appear to cast some doubt upon the efficiency of the immigration officials in Hong Kong, whether they be officials of the department in the class of civil servants or whether they be people employed on a part-time basis to assist in the investigation. This would seem to cast a great deal of doubt upon the entire structure of the immigration department which exists in Hong Kong, if that is where the bulk of these people came from. It would appear that it would not only cast some doubt upon the activities and efficiency of that branch in Hong Kong with respect to those who have entered Canada illegally but it might well cast doubt upon the opinions and decisions of that branch with respect to those applications which have been turned down.
