The hon. member for Cartier and also the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard made reference to section 39 of the act, and I would like to know who it is who has the final decision and discretion on these questions

of deportation, questions of admission and so on. Section 39 of the act was also cited in the reasons for judgment of Mr. Justice Norris in the matter of Miss Irene Rebrin. I forget the date, but it was recent anyhow. Section 39 of the act says:
No court and no judge or officer thereof has jurisdiction to review, quash, reverse, restrain or otherwise interfere with any proceeding, decision or order of the minister, deputy minister, director, immigration appeal board, special inquiry officer or immigration officer had, made or given under the authority and in accordance with the provisions of this act relating to the detention or deportation of any person, upon any ground whatsoever, unless such person is a Canadian citizen or has Canadian domicile.
If, as I read this section, final and complete authority is given to the minister to decide these cases, then I think this is far too much authority and power for the minister to have. That includes not only this minister but any minister, even the genius from Bonavista-Twillingate, and I am glad the hon. member for Cartier used that word in a sort of facetious way. If this is what this particular section means and it prevents any court from reviewing any particular case, then I think far too much authority is given, one, to the minister and, two, it is far too much for her or any other minister to ask for. Proceedings under this section would allow the minister and the government of which she is a member to be subjected to charges of discrimination, because if a person who is ordered to be deported is not given the reasons why he is being deported and he hears of another instance of a person who falls into somewhat the same category who should have been deported but was not, then he would ask himself why he was being deported and the other person allowed to stay.
This is the effect of this particular section of the act, that it places the minister in a very awkward and embarrassing position and subject to charges of discrimination and favouritism to one person over another. Mr. Justice Norris also made some comments about that. He said:
The provisions of this section constitute an attempt to bar recourse to the courts to all persons, other than Canadian citizens or persons having a Canadian domicile, who may consider themselves aggrieved by some decision of an immigration official, which attempt has been abortive only in part because of the determination of learned judges throughout Canada to ensure through the application of the prerogative writs of habeas corpus, certiorari and mandamus that the liberty of the stranger within our gates will be preserved.

Therefore, we can say that this figure, 19 per cent, has had nothing to do with the present unemployment situation either in Canada or in the province of Quebec; and the best proof of it is the fact that in the province of Ontario, where the great majority of immigrants have settled, unemployment is much lower than in the province of Quebec, where as I say, 19 per cent only of the immigrants have settled.

Share in Canada's great future. Reduced emigrant rates.
(Translation):
-which lists immediate job opportunities in Canada in about 75 trades, including jobs for bricklayers, butchers, carpenters, toolmakers, etc. I should like to know what the Quebec government authorities, who are friendly with the present federal government, think of that ridiculous invitation to
[Mr. Deschatelets.j
invite and admit, in Canada, immigrants whose livelihood depends upon their having jobs, while in the trades listed in that invitation, hundreds of thousands of Canadians are unemployed?
In that connection, Mr. Chairman, on May 25, 1960, the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) asked the following question:
(Text):
May I direct a question to the Prime Minister. In view of the high total of 787,000 unplaced applicants according to the figures released today by the dominion bureau of statistics, would the Prime Minister express his views today on the statement he made in London to the effect that our labour force will welcome at this time tens of thousands of immigrants?
The answer of the Prime Minister, as found at page 4222 of Hansard, was as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I have nothing to add to what has already been said in that connection.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, such a statement is a far cry from the demagogic advertisement I read at the beginning of my speech. Moreover, the surprising fact is that those two wrong interpretations come from the same family.
In any event, the third question is as follows: if, in the circumstances, the premier of Quebec sincerely feels that such an immigration policy, either under our administration or under the present administration, is harmful to the interest of the province of Quebec, why has he never mentioned the fact? Why did he never take up i the matter with the present government over the past four or five months? And why has he waited till just before the elections to raise the matter?
Moreover, if he was aware of the seriousness of this problem, why did the present Quebec premier, when he went to the Ontario legislature fail to express his views on this important national question?
I now ask our Conservative friends, especially the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville, to reply to these three questions: What do they think of the statement made by the Prime Minister before he left London, to the effect that this year, during this unemployment period, we could assimilate tens of thousands of immigrants? What do our Quebec friends, and especially our friend from Chambly-Rouville, think of the invitation published in December in the Belfast Telegraph asking tradesmen to come over here, when we had 700,000 unemployed and were unable to provide jobs for our Canadians? Moreover, what do they think of the stand taken

by Quebec provincial authorities regarding that insidious electoral advertisement published a few days ago which is contrary to the policy advocated for many years by their own party and their own leader?
Mr. Chairman, our immigration policy under the Liberal government, even during years of prosperity, was constantly being reviewed in the light of our requirements, of our assimilation capacity and of the economic situation changing from year to year. But, times have changed, and I suggest that in all fairness to the immigrants themselves, it is utterly ridiculous to allow into Canada immigrants who have to earn a living, when our tradesmen are now unemployed.
We must always consider this immigration question with great humanity and generosity, but also with a lot of good sense, according to present needs.
I had not meant to take part in the discussion on these estimates, but after seeing this demagogic election advertisement published in Quebec French language newspapers, but not in English language papers, I felt bound to answer those insidious claims; I owed it to the intelligence of Canadian and Quebec voters, and also to the truth.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have been very interested in this department for some time not because I know anybody who wants to come to Canada but because I have a number of Chinese people in my riding in whose problems I am very interested. I came to Ottawa three years ago expecting that eventually the government was going to do something, and particularly a new government which was pledged to equality, to eliminate discrimination and a number of other things. I expected they were going to do something, particularly in connection with the immigration department. I can tell you tonight, Mr. Chairman, that this government is not doing anything about that and is not capable of doing anything about it. In my opinion, they have not the intelligence even to know what is going on in that department. I am pleased to see these representatives from the department here tonight on their own time, and I think some of them ought to be here because I think some of them are connected with this problem that has developed in China, particularly in Hong Kong, and in my opinion some of them must have had some knowledge of this situation or it would not have gone on as it has.
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
I have seen letters written by the minister, by the Prime Minister and by other officials connected with the department, to Chinese people over the last three years telling them that there is going to be a revision that will be advantageous to them. The government is going to eliminate the discrimination that prevents them from bringing their relatives into this country. This is the type of information that has come to our attention over the last few years. This is a letter addressed to the minister and it is signed by Ruth Lok, chairman of the committee on immigration, C.C.A. In this letter she points out:
We understand that the Canadian Immigration Act is undergoing revision, and that views and criticisms concerning various sections can still be made with submissions as to how the act can become more equitable and democratic.
This is the type of letter I have seen go out to these Chinese people promising them that if they will be patient the act will be revised and some of the inequalities now affecting them will be changed to their advantage.
I am afraid I did not hear the name of the person who wrote this letter. I do not believe it came from my department.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: This was sent to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, parliament buildings: In the matter of certain revisions affecting the immigration to Canada of persons of Asian ancestry; submitted by the Chinese Canadian association and the national Japanese Canadian citizens association, 415 Spa-dina avenue, Toronto.
The hon. member says that I made these promises. Where is the document in which I made any promises?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I said I have seen letters written to the Chinese people, which they have shown me, and which are similar to this.
Produce them.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am not in any position to produce somebody else's mail. I have been shown these letters, and I have read them.
You never saw them.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You may never have seen them. You have not seen very much, anyway. You probably don't talk to any Chinese people. You are probably as backward and ignorant as these immigration people.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman; it seems to me that before the hon. member goes any further along this line I want to say right now that I have not

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration written any letters to any members of the Chinese community telling them I would make revisions in their favour.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I cannot contradict that. I will try to produce the letters. I think I can.
Yes you do that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I will certainly get photostatic copies of them. They will not be exactly as the minister says because I did not say that. I said that they were going to be to their advantage, and they would probably solve their particular problem. I never suggested, and I am not suggesting now, that the minister herself promised these people relief in specific cases.
You just said it.
That is what you said.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Not in specific cases, but in a general way. Certainly this is the impression these organizations gained as is indicated by the letter I have just read. I have seen these letters. I have received this information over a period of three years.
I have been advised quite recently that if people of Asiatic descent want to bring their relations in, whom they felt it was advisable to bring in, they should bring them in exactly in the manner a lot of Chinese people have had to come into this country, that is to pay their money and bring them in through the back door. I think this is the way it is being done. If we use the figure of 11,000, and it has not been disputed by the departmental officials, and use the figure 1 have seen of $3,000, that means $33 million worth of graft some place. I would suggest that the government and the department cannot be so ignorant of the situation that they do not know this goes on.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member stated that this figure of 11,000 had not been disputed by the department. The Minister of Justice disputed that in the house not so long ago and said that this was not an official figure at all. I just want that brought to your attention.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: This afternoon the minister said her department had neither confirmed nor denied it.
I am stating what the Minister of Justice said.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
We did not discuss the matter with the Minister of Justice. I did not hear him make that statement, but I did hear the minister responsible for this department


make the statement to which I have referred. It seems to me we should make up our minds whether or not we want Chinese, Japanese, and in fact Asiatics in Canada. It is very unfair to hold this carrot out in front of the Asiatic people and tell them that if certain conditions are met, and we hope to meet them immediately, we hope to eliminate this discrimination and then you will be allowed to come into the country. This seems to me to be very unfair and to be a discriminatory way of treating these people.
We all know that there are people in Canada who would say that we have to bring in so many British for every one we bring in of French ancestry; that we would have to bring in so many Portuguese for every Italian we bring in. There are people who calculate exactly the composition of the Canadian population they want in the next five or ten years. In my opinion, this is not the honest or fair way of doing it. It is even more unfair when we tell people that we are going to change the act, that we are going to change the discriminatory clauses in the act so it will permit equality.
I hope some hon. members have taken the opportunity of reading just what the act does say. The Chinese and Japanese people have given close consideration to the various sections of the act. This is a brief presented by the Chinese benevolent association in 1958. They may have presented other briefs since that time, but if they have I do not happen to have a copy. Perhaps they agree with me that there does not seem to be a dam bit of sense in bringing a brief to a government which has already promised to do what you are asking but has no intention of doing it.
In the brief they point out the particular classes that can come in. They go into the history of the Asiatic people who first came to Canada, their reasons for coming and the services they rendered to the Canadian people. Then they point out on page 3 that racial discrimination still exists in the immigration law. The brief goes on to say:
In the briefs presented to your predecessors, it was pointed out that the discriminatory nature of these laws has created great hardships for many families of Chinese Canadians who fled the communist regime in China and who are now living in Hong Kong in the hope that they may be reunited with husbands and parents.
I have here some place the break-down of the classes of people that are allowed to come to Canada from some countries, and those from Asiatic countries who are not allowed to come. The qualifying parts of the act are found in section 20, as amended by

order in council P.C. 1957/1675-Hansard, January 25, 1958-which states as follows:
Amendment to immigration regulation P.C. 19541351. P.C. 1957-1675 of December 20, 1957, revokes paragraph (d) of section 20 and substitutes the following therefor:
"a person who is a citizen of a country other than a country referred to in paragraphs (a), (b) or (c) or in section 21, if such a person is the husband, the wife or the unmarried child under 21 years of age, the father where he is over 65 years of age, or the mother where she is over 60 years of age, of a Canadian citizen or of a person legally admitted to Canada for permanent residence who is residing in Canada and who has applied for and is in a position to receive and care for any such person, but no such child shall be landed in Canada unless his father or his mother, as the case may be, is landed in Canada concurrently with him."
Then the brief goes on to say this:
The fundamental structure of the Canadian immigration policy stresses the union of the family. However, when section 20, as set forth in the above paragraph, is carefully scrutinized, the act reveals preference for the families of one country against those of another. Why, in this democratic country of Canada should a Canadian act differentiate and discriminate on grounds of race, colour, or ancestry?
It is true the Canadian immigration department has recognized the need for family unity and has provided for relatives of certain Canadians to be admitted into Canada by section 20, paragraphs
(c) and (d) of the act. However, there is a disparity, between paragraphs (c) and (d), which restricts the interpretation of what constitutes a family if it is of Asian ancestry.
We respectfully submit that, if the section is carefully examined, for every 16 categories of persons admitted through paragraph (c), only five are admitted through paragraph (d). We respectfully submit the following chart which is a breakdown of the categories contained in section 20 (c) and (d).
It shows the 16 categories in the one class and for Asiatics only five particular classes. It also goes on to say this:
Furthermore, although the ratio is 16 to 5, section 20 (d) is further limited in that it states, "No such child shall be landed in Canada unless his father or his mother, as the case may be, is landed in Canada concurrently with him", and limits parents, "Mother must be 60 years or over, and father must be 65 years of age or over."
It is evident that a Canadian whose ancestry falls into section 20 (c) has the privilege of forging a much wider family tie than has a Canadian whose ancestry falls into section 20 (d).
We take this opportnuity to reveal the hardship Canadians, whose ancestry comes under section 20
(d)	, have suffered due to the inequality in the Immigration Act. The cases appended to this brief have been submitted to the Japanese association with the hope that the applicant will be united to his or her kin from Asia.
Anyway this gives you an indication of how discriminatory this is. These people are appealing not to the old Liberal government, which was a decaying government which had been here too long and had become set in its ways and certainly had no intention of changing its mind at all; they are appealing to a new government under the leadership
9, 1960
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration of John Diefenbaker, the sponsor of a bill of rights for the Canadian people. How can this parliament grant a bill of rights to the Canadian people by law and at the same time have on the statute books laws that are as discriminatory against Canadian people as are these particular laws?
Will the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Surely.

Does the hon. member
believe in practical rights for Canadians in the province of Quebec?
Just as much as you do.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: If I answered that question, Mr. Chairman, I think we would be a mile off the subject.
You are off it anyway.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Reference is being made to a debate that is continuing in this house on a different subject altogether.
You would be closer than you are now to the matter before the committee.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
What I would suggest is this. If the government wishes to introduce a divorce debate into the discussion of the immigration estimates, I have not found any place in this house where it properly belongs. This might be the place for they have so many other things in this department and they might have a divorce section, for all I know.
One of the problems the minister has not faced but with which they are faced is this. I know that she is a reasonable woman and I am quite sure she is doing her best in her department. However, she inherited an unholy mess and this mess had built up over many years and the civil service that were responsible for this mess have been doing the same things for many years. The newspapers indicate it may perhaps have been for 10 years. I expect it may go even further back than that. But the Liberals had a solution for this problem. When they found somebody who was very favourable to them they passed an order in council that admitted two or three people in this manner in several little ways in which they could go around the act and leave the act as bad as it was. I think the Chinese people in my area were sincere when they believed there were going to be amendments and that they were going to be major amendments that were going to be to their advantage because they were tired of playing around with this business of $3,000.
Mr. Chairman, while $3,000 is a great deal of money to me, I have in my community

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Chinese people who could afford close to $3 million if they wanted to spend it and who have the money to spend. The people that they would bring in would be no liability to Canada. One of them who has been brought in, incidentally, by one of the parties who are still trying to bring in relatives, is a civil servant here in Ottawa, and he is quite a high civil servant. He has been a credit to himself, to his people and his ancestors. It would appear to me that they believe they can stay within the law and that the new government will change the act and allow more leniency and a little better deal for them to bring in their relatives and their friends.
I have one particular Chinese constituent who wants to bring in his daughter-in-law and family. As I understand it, the son was killed and he now wants to bring the daughter-in-law into the family. This case has been going back and forth in the department for a number of years. I firmly believe that there is not much point in my writing to the minister and asking for any consideration in this case because, according to my understanding of it, it does not come under the terms of the act as we now operate. If these people were of any other nationality they could come into this country.
There are other people who are in almost as bad a position and these are West Indies people, particularly people from the British colonies in the West Indies. I have in my riding a very good friend who was obliged to change his religion, to all intents and purposes, in order to get into this country. It was impossible for him to come in with the religion he had so he changed it. He was Jewish previously, and now officially he is an Anglican and is still practising the faith of his fathers. He was obliged to tell the immigration department that he was an Anglican and that his wife was an Anglican or they could not get in here. He had tried t previously and failed but when he was willing to change his religion, then he got into the country. I would suggest that he is a good citizen with a good background. His father was one of the best known citizens of the particular island from which he came.
In the last list the department has put out I notice that no people are listed as coming from Jamaica and some of the other islands. I would not know under what they would be listed; maybe it would be "other origins". If so, there are not many of them anyway, because under all other origins in the first quarter of this year there were only 702 people and this may include people from the West Indies. I do not know.
It seems to me that we can stand a great number of people in Canada. I have noticed

in the papers where Canada is to allow more refugees into the country, and I would like to know from the department whether we asked these refugees to come in because we wanted them to fit into our plans, or did we want them to come in because our Secretary of State for External Affairs is a strong willed person and decided, when he heard the appeals made, that these people could be welcomed into Canada? Did he say, "We will bring them in here and I will talk the Prime Minister and others into my way of thinking"?
I rather think that these refugees came in through the grace of our external affairs minister rather than any other way. This is a good thing. I do not think it hurts to bring in this sort of refugee. I do not think it hurts when someone asks to bring in some relations from Austria or Hungary or one of those countries, relations who had t.b. and are now considered cured and can get four or five doctors to testify that they are cured and ask that some consideration be given to them. People are willing to put up a bond that the refugees will not become a responsibility. Why should not citizens who have been living here who are 30 or 40 years old and who have a mother of 60 or 70 not be allowed to bring her in instead of looking after her in a country where they have no connections and where there are increasing difficulties about sending money?
It would seem to me that a number of departments in this government need to be broken up, and this department is one. The department could be broken up into citizenship and immigration. There is some similarity between the two departments but I think we could concentrate after we get the immigrants here on whether they become good citizens or not and we could make better citizens out of them if we treated them better when we brought them here.
We have had an advertisement appearing in one of our papers which has made my people real mad. We have a large number of new Canadians in northern Ontario. Many of them came from Scotland and Ireland and they have to listen to this kind of junk. Whoever wrote this advertisement must have been hired for his literary ability, because they certainly did not hire him for his honesty. I would not say that anything in here is dishonest but I would say that the facts are vastly distorted. It is true that we do have new homes and beautiful suburbs, but this does not mean that somebody leaving a good job in Scotland could come to Canada and a week after find himself in a beautiful suburb living in a $15,000, a $20,000 or a $30,000 house, because he will not. He will

live in a shack like those in many communities and work on jobs which are only half as well paid as the job he had before, and his standard of living will be lower. This is true of hundreds of people in the mining field and as soon as some save some money they trot back home and wish they had never left home.
Mr. Chairman, among the companies who are mentioned in this particular advertisement are the Canadian Pacific Steamship Lines. Then there was another advertisement from Toronto which referred to the city travel agencies, a theatre company, the Cunard lines, the Canadian film board and the immigration service. I do not know whether all c these people paid for this three quarter page advertisement which appeared in the London Daily Mail, but this article says:	"This
article has been contributed by the Canadian government immigration service."
Mr. Chairman, if we paid for this let us at least be honest about what Canada is. We have a large unemployment situation here. We have many problems in housing, in the medical services and hospitalization which we have not been able to solve yet. Let us not paint this sort of picture which will mean that when people come here they will distrust and dislike us for having lured them here under false pretences. Let us be honest and tell the people over there what Canada really means, and if it means rotation, let us rotate.
It seems to me that we must do something to correct all these problems, and I would suggest a real shake-up in this department is necessary and that a good place to start it would be in this particular item dealing with immigration. I suggest that we should do what we did with the Chinese problem, which is an important one now because we do not know how bad it is. I am sure that people will still go on collecting $3,000 and bringing people in through the back door. Our laws are so bad that they make law-abiding and honest citizens break the laws in order to accomplish what they think is morally just and morally right.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman in his concluding remarks repeated a statement that he made earlier, and if he had not been a relatively young and inexperienced member I would have challenged him the moment he made it. He said it was customary-and he implied he knew of many cases-for people to pay $3,000 to get other people into this country by the back door. I should like to ask the hon. gentleman, if he knew of any such cases, whether he did his duty as a citizen and informed the police and, if he did not, why not?

This is a very serious charge that the hon. gentleman has made. He got up here and talked about officials who were here in the house and not allowed to speak for themselves. I have been in that kind of position in the past, sir. I have heard members of parliament get up and attack civil servants who could not reply, and I have absolutely no respect for members of parliament who use their parliamentary immunity to attack people who cannot reply. If these brave members who make these charges here, where they are not answerable in the courts, would make them to the police and produce the evidence, it would be a lot better for this country and for the public affairs of this country.
Hear, hear.

I had the responsibility for the last three years the former government was in office of the administration of this department, and every charge and suggestion of any kind of impropriety that was ever made was investigated and investigated immediately. Charges were laid in the courts in a few regrettable cases, quite a few in one particular instance, and there were others. Disciplinary action was taken by this department in a manner that was a credit to the public service of Canada, which is not filled with a lot of loafers and corrupt people as the hon. gentleman, in his loose way, suggested.
Hear, hear.

I think it is time we had an end to this kind of talk. If a citizen has not the courage to lay the information and all the information he has before the police, then if he knows of wrongdoing he should not come in here and hide under his immunity and attack people who cannot reply. I think as far as I am concerned I have nothing but contempt for that kind of conduct.
Now, sir, I had not really intended-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Do you want an answer?
The hon. gentleman can answer in his own time when I have finished; I did not interrupt him.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You said you asked a question.
If the hon. gentleman would like to answer he may.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this particular problem has concerned me for some time. I know of people who have been reported to have come in in this particular manner. 1 know of one particular family which we mentioned to the department but got no satisfaction from them. The department has always

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration said that they appreciate the information and will investigate it. I have no idea whether it was correct or not. My Chinese informants still tell me this is correct in this particular case.
I did go to the department a week or two before the arrests were made in Hong Kong and repeated these charges. I said I was advising my people not to wait for the amendments but to go ahead and pay their $3,000. I informed the department there and talked to the head of the department who was handling the matter, and it was only a week or so after that the arrests were made in Hong Kong and the charges began there.
I think the hon. gentleman has answered himself and perhaps it is unnecessary for me to say anything further about this subject.
I think so too.

The point I really want to talk about particularly is a quarrel I have with the minister. It is one that I have had ever since the hon. lady made a statement in this chamber which I thought was a very foolish statement, which I said at the time I though was a very foolish statement and which in the light of experience has proved to be not only a very foolish thing but a very inhuman thing that has worked a great deal of unnecessary hardship on a number of people who would make perfectly good immigrants and citizens.
I believe the minister knows very well to what I am referring. I refer to the statement she made on August 23, 1958 as reported at page 4033 of Hansard. She said:
An increased number of non-immigrants have, after entry, applied for permanent residence in Canada. Many of them have obtained employment.
And so on. The hon. lady spoke at some length and I shall not take the time to read it in full. However, I do not want to paraphrase incorrectly and I will be glad to make any correction the hon. lady asks me to make because I do not want to be unfair about this. The minister indicated quite clearly that all those persons then in the country as visitors would be processed as though they had applied from outside the country but from that day onward, anyone who came here as a visitor would not be allowed to apply for landing in Canada but would have to go home and apply there. If the minister thinks I have not summarized it fairly I invite her to say so now.
In reply to the minister on that occasion I said:
I should now like to make a comment or two about the announcement made by the hon. lady. What her announcement amounted to when

stripped of all its verbiage is that instead of considering each application individually as has been the case in the past she is attempting to establish a cut-off date so as to consider all these cases at once and then apply all the full rigours of the law after March X.
That would be March 1, 1959. I continue:
Having dealt with those cases as they arose over a period of some three years, I can understand why any minister would seek to formalize the procedure and reduce the amount of agony connected with it, but I would not like the hon. lady to get away with the impression that this represents any liberalization of the policy of the department because it is in fact the precise reverse.
I then went on to say something that subsequently proved to be incorrect. I said that I did not think the minister would be successful in maintaining her cut-off date but so far the hon. lady-perhaps because of those Dutch characteristics to which my friend the hon. member for Cartier referred earlier- has stubbornly persisted in that policy except in a few cases I know about.
I may say that same matter came up at the time the estimates of the department were before the estimates committee in 1955. It was raised at that time by the hon. member for Oxford. I have the proceedings here. The date appears to have been February 28, 1955 and I refer to page 83 of the proceedings. At that time the following exchange occurred between the hon. member for Oxford and myself:

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Along the same line, with respect to the procedure in the case of a proposed immigrant to Canada who has resided in Canada but as a non-immigrant; suppose he files an application and then is told that he must go back to his own country and make an application from there; could he not submit his application while in Canada on a temporary basis?
I understand that it all depends on the circumstances; sometimes they are processed while he is still in Canada and sometimes they are told that they should go back and make an application.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Could the minister give us any indication or idea as to people who are resident in Canada on a non-immigrant basis, and when they are told they have to go back to their original country to make their application?
At that point Mr. Smith who was then the director of immigration gave the following answer:

That is not done as a rule with the ones who are here, when we are satisfied that their intention when they came was not to circumvent any of our requirements. But we also advise them that their examination will take much longer in Canada than it would if they returned or if they returned to their own country of origin because of the procedures which have to be gone through, and that they can be dealt with much more rapidly on their return than would be the case if they remained here. However we do not insist on them going back if we are satisfied that the man is to be dealt with favourably here, and if he can comply with our requirements and regulations.

The discussion continued:

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: So it depends on the individual case?
That is right.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Suppose a person comes from the United States. In all cases probably he would be able to be accepted rather than to have to go back to the United States and apply?
Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Whereas a person who comes from Italy or France might even have to go back to Italy or France to get through more quickly?
I replied to that question and this is the reply I wish particularly to draw to your attention, Mr. Chairman:

Perhaps I might say a word about my own experience as minister in this matter. It is not very conclusive,-
I might say at that time I had been minister for only six or seven months. I continue:
-but I think that there is a disposition on the part of the departmental officers, when someone has come in here as a non-immigrant with what looks pretty clearly like the deliberate intention of beating the regulations, to say, "Well, you can't do this; you have to go back and take your chances like the other people in the country you came from." But when someone comes genuinely as a visitor, likes this country and wants to stay, and looks like a person who in all probability might satisfy the regulations if he were processed, our disposition is not to suggest their return, I say that this is just the impression that I have obtained as minister from having dealt with cases of that kind. That is the kind of case that comes to me most often.
I believe the attitude I took at that time was the right and proper attitude to be taken. I know it is much easier administratively to say "no" to all these cases, to say to every visitor who comes to Canada, "You came here as a visitor; we do not know whether or not you are qualified as an immigrant; go back and put yourself on an equal basis with someone who has never been here." But this often involves months of time, maybe more than a year. It involves the disruption of people's lives and, in many cases, it involves fairly great expense. I have never been able to see how any member of the public who, after all, we represent here and whose servants we are or ought to be, could ever understand why we would say to people concerning whom there may be reasonable grounds for thinking they are perfectly qualified to be landed as immigrants, "You have to spend hundreds or thousands of dollars to go back where you came from and make your application in that country," instead of processing the applications here.
I know from the experience I have had and from the very kind of experience that the hon. lady has had this afternoon that every so often you get a difficult case that you feel you should turn down and that you have a duty imposed by this parliament to turn down. In the final analysis it is the duty 79951-0-300i

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration of the minister imposed by a statute of this parliament to make decisions of that kind.
I had no hand in drafting that act although I had three years of administering it. I do not see how else the matter can be handled. I wish I could see some other way. I suppose it would be possible to establish or erect some kind of administrative tribunal to deal with these things. I have thought a great deal about that. If that were done I hope it would never be done on a basis that would allow an appeal to the minister. I hope that if an administrative tribunal were established -and that would have to be done by parliament itself, it could not be done by any regulations under the existing law because the existing law says the minister must decide; the courts have ruled in the Brent case that in the final analysis no one but the minister can decide-there would be no appeal to the minister and therefore, as I say, if we want to change it to establish an administrative tribunal it would have to be done by act of parliament.
I think very serious consideration should be given to all the implications of that, but I know what would happen. I know it would be said at once that the people appearing before this tribunal had not been properly treated and there would be appeals to the minister to reverse the tribunal. I would hope that we would decide either that there is going to be a tribunal which will have the final say or leave the matter with the minister. That, as I say, is something that cannot be settled here and now.
But I do appeal to the minister very strongly to reverse that decision which she made, and that is all it was. There was no order in council; it was just a decision by the minister and by the department. I ask her to go back to the system of considering here in Canada the cases of visitors on their merits. Nothing else makes any kind of sense to ordinary people.
I should like to say at the same time that I do not think there is a disposition in the case of persons who do not technically qualify under the law and the regulations as they stand at the present time to take a somewhat restrictive view. Of course, the governor in council could admit such cases on the recommendation of the minister. But there is a disposition now in certain cases to be unnecessarily rigid. One hon. member who spoke this afternoon-it may have been the hon. member for Cartier or the hon. member for Vancouver Centre-said something about half-sisters. Half-sisters are not unique creatures, but they are not in the common, ordinary run. There are not so many of them and there have been a few cases where it
4758	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration seems to me that by making a liberal interpretation of policy no one would have been harmed. It may be that the law makes it impossible for the department to admit such cases, but it would not be impossible for the governor in council to make one of these exceptional rulings such as I think ought to be made from time to time.
This brings up what I know from experience to be one of the most difficult problems in the administration of the Immigration Act. I read the proceedings of the committee when the act was revised in 1951 or 1952 before I was a member of parliament. I read them with great care. I read the debates in the house, and I know that there are different ways of administering immigration. I can see only three possible ways of administering immigration. One way-the easiest way- would be to let anybody come here who wanted to come, without demanding any kind of qualifications whatsoever. I would give any government that attempted to introduce a policy of that kind just about as much time as it takes me to snap my fingers to stay in office. I do not believe there is any hon. member who would have the foolhardiness to suggest such a policy in this house, because we all know it would never be acceptable to the Canadian people. What I am about to say is, no doubt, not a very wise thing to say, politically, and I will no doubt be attacked as an old-fashioned reactionary for saying it. But there is no doubt that a great many people use arguments about immigration as though that should be the policy. They have not, however, got the courage to say it should be the policy. They talk loosely about discrimination of one kind and another, but if you put it right to them and say: are you in favour of an open-door policy, they would, of course, shy away from it.
In the absence of an open-door policy it is, of course, necessary to have some criteria of selection. That is all there is in the regulations which, as the hon. member for Timiskaming has correctly pointed out, are the same as they were when I was in office. Perhaps I would not defend them if they were not. They are the same as they were, and a tremendous amount of thought was given to them. I do not think they are perfect. But what was really sought was to make them practical so that they could deal with all the ordinary cases and all the ordinary problems one encountered.
We must remember this: the moment you have any criteria of selection you have to rely on human beings to do the selecting and you will always get these people who will refer to officials as little tyrants, as the Prime


Minister used to do when he was sitting over here. I notice the right hon. gentleman does not say that any more. Of course, he has much more important things to think of now.
The plain fact is that if you have any criteria of selection at all you must have human beings to perform that function, and they are going to make mistakes. There is, of course, one other way and that is the United States system of the establishment of quotas. I do not know on what basis the Canadian people would ever agree to the establishment of quotas. I think we would have a very hard time indeed getting agreement in this country on a quota system and on what quota should be given to whom. No one who has ever had any responsibility for the administration of immigration since immigration began as a government service in this country has ever attempted it.
I really think there are times when we ought to look at the fundamentals of these things and see what we are really talking about. I believe that on balance the system we now have of making it almost open for those people who are most like ourselves to enter this country is probably the best system we could adopt at the present time. When I say "people who are most like ourselves" I do not mean that we are superior, or any nonsense of that sort. I say that because I believe that such people can adapt themselves to the country faster. For one thing, they do not have to learn the language. That is not saying that immigrants of this sort are superior to others. It is just that it is easier for them to integrate.
Immigration costs the receiving countries something, too. I have been very much impressed by some hon. gentlemen who are inclined sometimes to talk out of both sides of their mouths on this question. They talk about unemployment and the desirability of keeping people out, then they complain bitterly because some people are kept out. You have to make up your mind one way or the other. My own view is that in times when there is considerable unemployment and where people cannot get jobs easily we should not have open placement immigration at all. By that, I mean the immigration of people who have no connection with Canada.
I also am an unrepentant believer in the system of sponsorship which I think has served Canada exceedingly well since it was adopted in 1947 as a principle of immigration. I do not care what race a man comes from; a person who comes here with a brother or a father or a son or a cousin living in Canada to help him over the first hard period is going to find it easier to get along, and will

make a contribution to this country faster than someone who knows nobody here and is a complete stranger.
If instead of trying to find reasons for complaint in regard to the present regulations we approached them from the viewpoint of understanding why they were designed in the way they are, it would be found, I think, that what they seek to do is to make it as easy as possible for the close relatives of all those who live in this country to come here and join them.
I referred earlier today and I want to refer again to the fact that we had the liberality in this country-I am not claiming credit for this particularly for the government to which I belonged because it was before I belonged to it anyway and it would not have been done if the people of Canada had not been willing to accept it-to go on admitting the relatives of our Chinese Canadian citizens. I am proud of the fact that we did, that we did not allow the kind of passions which in an earlier period sometimes disfigured these matters to have sway, that, all during the period of the Korean war we admitted these Chinese immigrants with relatives here who were citizens. No other country in the world did that kind of thing. We are told that there was discrimination and so on; yes, there was discrimination, but I do not think it was discrimination in a bad sense. Because we had a good loyal population of Chinese Canadians it was favourable discrimination to say that we could safely admit their close relatives, and I think the proof of that pudding has been in the eating.
With respect to the 23,000 who have come, notwithstanding what anybody may say I do not believe that half of them came here illegally, and unless I see the evidence in black and white in each individual case and examine it I will not believe it at all. I am certainly not going to believe it on any kind of hearsay. I think it is most unfortunate. I do not believe that $44 million or $33 million was paid to bring these people here. I think stories like that are just utter and unadulterated rubbish and anybody who knows how hard it is to raise $44 million ought to know that.
I said in 1955 and again in 1956 that I was sure, because of the inherent difficulties in this matter, that nobody can remove and that no system could remove, that some people who were not relatives at all would be able to get through the net and that there would be some cases of fraud. I have felt all along that there were, and I do not care how many categories you have or what categories you have, there would still be some. When there is the kind of pressure that there is in this particular situation there will be
9, 1960	4759
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration a temptation to commit fraud. But before we start tossing around loose charges about these matters it does seem to me that we should know the facts and really have the information about them.
I should also like to say something else about the administration of the Immigration Act that I said before and that the hon. lady has not received very well when I have said it before. She received it exceptionally badly the last time I said it. I hope she will refrain from the temptation tonight to give the reply which she gave last year and the year before, and in order to discourage her from doing so I am going to give it first. It is true she can find in the files that when I was minister I did order some people deported who had children who were Canadian citizens. There is no doubt that some of these people either left voluntarily or were deported. 1 am ashamed of that, so there is no need for the hon. lady to say anything about it. I have said that publicly in the house before and I say it again. It was a mistake I made, and I think we should make it abundantly clear, no matter where we sit in the house that regardless of what their record is we do not intend to deport the parents of infant Canadian citizens.
What are we doing when we do that? We are putting on another country the responsibility for infant citizens of this country who were born here and who will never lose their citizenship unless they do so as a voluntary act, because no Canadian born citizen can lose his citizenship except by accepting the citizenship of another country. What we are doing is sending into exile our own citizens or separating them from their parents and thereby probably making them public charges. In a country like Canada with its wealth and its need for people, if we occasionally get some people who are technically deportable, or even bad people, and who happen to be the parents of Canadian citizens I believe we should not deport them when these Canadian citizens are infants and have to be cared for by someone. I should like to see the law changed so that this could not be done. But the law does not need to be changed. All the hon. lady needs to do is to change her mind or, if it is not her mind, to change the minds of her colleagues in order to have this done.
There is one other thing I want to say, Mr. Chairman, and I can see that you are looking at the clock. I must say I am exceedingly disappointed at the entirely unresponsive attitude of the Prime Minister-I do not blame the hon. lady for this but rather put the blame where it belongs, on the Prime Minister-to the appeal of the Canadian

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration welfare council and all sorts of Canadians all over the country who want to make a voluntary contribution to world refugee year. The Canadian welfare council made certain suggestions to the Prime Minister months ago, and I think I have asked him on an average of every 10 days when the government is going to reach a decision about this matter. On each occasion I have received the usual kind of answer that, unhappily, we get from the Prime Minister about matters of public policy most of the time.
The fact of the matter is that as long as we impose upon private sponsors of refugees an indefinite responsibility for the health and welfare care of these refugees we virtually make it impossible for them to be sponsored. While we have made great professions of our desire to do something about this matter, we have carefully kept the regulations in such a state that they really are a practical prohibition to action except in the case of people who either are very wealthy or very careless about their obligations.
The welfare council suggested that the government should get in touch with the provinces and reach some agreement. I personally do not think that was the best approach that could have been made. I think it would not be too much for the government of Canada to say in the case of sponsored refugees that, after a year or two years, the government would undertake the residual responsibility for health and welfare care. It would not amount to very much. If sponsors have to do it for a year or two years they are not going to assume terrible responsibilities, and it does seem to me that this would break the log jam in this whole business. We still have three weeks before the end of world refugee year and I appeal once more to the government to take a constructive attitude about this matter or at least to make up its mind and give a definite answer.

Mr. Chairman, first of all may I thank the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate on two scores; first, for rising so ably to the defence of my staff and thereby saving me the trouble of doing so and, second, for having given some very constructive and frank comments on administration. I must say that in some cases I do not agree with him but that is to be expected. If I may answer his last remarks first, I should like to tell him that so far as the sponsorship of refugees is concerned we


believe that the program is coming along very well. As the Prime Minister said, we do not intend to stop it at the end of world refugee year. He will be interested to know that, we have had about 80 applications for private sponsorship which have been developed, and several of these people are already in Canada. This comprises somewhere around 150 persons. The volume of inquiries has been very heavy, and in most cases the sponsors are groups of people.
I indicated earlier, I think, in response to a question asked by the hon. member for Essex East, that a meeting was arranged with the minister of health for Ontario, Dr. Dymond, to discuss the detailed implications of the statement made by Premier Frost on April 12 last respecting the Ontario government's part in assistance to refugees. I am glad to say that fas a result of the discussions which were held with Dr. Dymond on May 30 last we have now received a communication in which Dr. Dymond states, on behalf of the Ontario government, and I quote:
-while the province cannot undertake responsibility for any costs involved in the transportation of immigrant refugees, we will be prepared to assume the normally accepted welfare costs after the immigrant refugees have been in our province for six months.
What this means is that while the provincial authorities of Ontario cannot, for understandable reasons, accept responsibility for transportation costs, or for assistance given to an immigrant refugee during the first six months of his residence in Ontario, they have undertaken to provide to such immigrant refugees at the end of six months the normal assistance services available to ordinary residents of the province. Transportation arrangements, therefore, together with any assistance that may be necessary to an immigrant refugee during the first six months of his stay in Ontario will continue, in sponsored cases, to be the responsibility of the individual, group or agency providing sponsorship.
I think it will be recognized that the position taken by the province of Ontario in regard to this matter will be very helpful to those individuals or groups who are considering the possible sponsorship of immigrant refugee cases. I am hopeful that as a result of the initiative taken in this matter by Ontario other provinces will follow suit, and I am sure that this will greatly facilitate the possibilities of moving a larger number of immigrant refugees to Canada under suitable sponsorship arrangements than might otherwise have been possible.
This was action which we took as a result of the representations made by the Canadian

welfare council and others. I think it will work out very well. We are certainly going to give it a try, in any event.
The hon. member had something to say with reference to the deportation of the parents of Canadian born babies. I do not intend to get into any detailed argument. I feel strongly that it is a wrong principle to permit these people to stay here simply because a child is born in Canada. I should like to quote a portion of the judgment rendered in one case by the superior court of Quebec. I should like to quote three paragraphs which I feel set out rather well the thinking of the court at that time with which, I must say, I agree.
It is not true that the deportation of her parents will deprive this child of her Canadian citizenship. Not only is it not against "public order, good morals and Christian charity" that she should follow her parents in the country of which her parents and herself are citizens, but it would be indeed against "public order, good morals and Christian charity" that her parents abstain from taking her with them. In this respect, the fate of this child will be no better nor worse than that of a child bom of Canadian parents in a country where, by reason of his having been born there, he is entitled to citizenship of that country, nor than that of a Canadian child of Canadian parents who decide to emigrate from Canada.
By taking the child with them, her parents would not be taking her into exile as she would still be living in a country of which she is a citizen having been born of Haitian citizens.
The hon. member will recognize the case.
To accept this extraordinary and astounding argument of petitioners in support of their objection to deportation of themselves would amount to admitting that the birth of a child to persons not being citizens of this country but residing here temporarily entitles ipso facto the parents to become Canadan citizens, a principle which manifestly would be contrary to the spirit, purposes and provisions of our law.
I think, Mr. Chairman, I could not improve upon that in any way, and I will leave it at that.
Well, the hon. lady can have it.

All right. There were several matters raised in the course of the debate this afternoon. I think I might comment on a few of them at this time. The hon. member for Cartier had quite a bit to say about the advertising which was done in the United Kingdom and asked, I think, why it was not done in some other countries.
He asked whether it was done in other countries.

The simple answer to that is that in most of the European countries we are not permitted to advertise. Most of the * European countries do not permit us to do any real promotional advertising for immigration. If the hon. member is interested in
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration any one country I will try to tell him what the situation is. It just happens that the United Kingdom is one place where we can and do advertise. I should say that the advertisements which have been quoted here today have been, in the main, old ones. They have not been recent. There has been no advertising in the last few months. The advertisements which were quoted by one hon. member were those of a transportation company, not ours.
It is true that a few months ago there would be a few classifications of employment for which there was a demand in Canada listed in these advertisements. These classifications are taken from the experiences of our offices across Canada after consultation with officials of the national employment service. Having said that, I think I should go further and say that it is true that there might be unemployment in a given line of work in one part of the country and still be vacancies in that particular line of work in another part of the country. People are not too likely to tear up roots. They are naturally optimistic and hope that in a few months things will be better. They tend to stay where they are, particularly if they own their own homes and have families. They are reluctant to move thousands of miles away from the cities in which they reside. In that respect it is quite possible that we have openings for persons in a given line of employment in one of the eastern Ontario cities, whereas in the same line of work there will be people unemployed in a western city. That is, broadly, the explanation.
I should like to reply to the hon. member for Vancouver East in this regard and tell him that we are not sending open placement immigrants to British Columbia except in these specific cases; in the professional classes; butchers and meatcutters, they tell me there is a limited demand for them in British Columbia; bakers, pastry cooks and cooks, and there is a limited demand for them. There is a good demand for domestics, nurses' aides and waiters. These are the only ones that are being directed to British Columbia. I thought the hon. member might be interested in that information.
I should also tell the hon. member for Cartier, with regard to his inquiry about deportations to Iraq, that there have been no deportations to Iraq in the last three years. I do not know whether he is aware of that.
I am pleased to hear that.

I think probably the information upon which he based his argument was older than three years. With regard to deportations in general, may I say for the information of several hon. members of the

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration committee who have mentioned this matter that in the last three years these deportations have numbered 150 per year less than they did in the preceding three years.
Will the hon. lady permit a question?
Certainly.
She knows, as do I, that "deportations" is a loose word. Are these deportations of landed immigrants, deportations of visitors or all deportations?

This particular figure had to do with all deportations. However, if the hon. member would like to have the figures with respect ot others, I can give them to him. In the last three years the deportations executed were 1,924. No, I am sorry; the information I gave is wrong. The figure 150 has to do with just those who were in the country, not border exclusions.
The hon. lady knows there are two kinds of so-called deportations. When the act is changed I hope she will take note of them and use a different word.
Exclusions, you mean? *
I feel that deportation should be reserved only for immigrants who have been landed and where they have, of course, a legal process to go through. That is what I was really interested in.
The deportations that were executed have to do with people who were in the country. I do not know whether we have those separated into immigrants and non-immigrants.
It does not really matter.

However, they were not border exclusions. In that case there were 1,924 in the last three years and in the years preceding there were 2,370, which is an average of 150 per year less in the recent period.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to hold up this debate unduly but


there are one or two matters pertaining to sponsored immigration with which I should like to deal very briefly at this time. However, before I proceed I should like to say, in fairness to the minister and her staff that over the years I have had excellent co-operation from both the minister and her staff in Ottawa and also her staff at Niagara Falls, Ontario, which is the port of entry for the Niagara peninsula.
The matter with which I wish to deal, as I say, is sponsored immigration. Under the regulations at the present time a person who is a Canadian can bring to this country from, say, Poland a brother or a sister and his or her family. But in some cases where there is one or more members in the family over 18 years of age you run into a serious problem because it appears that under the regulations there is no specific provision to sponsor such a person.
I have had one or two cases of that kind. I might say that in one case when the man who was making the application in Niagara Falls was told that one member of the family, a girl just over 18, could not come in, he dropped the application. In another case the application went through, the family came here and a daughter was left in Poland hoping that after a while she would be able to come.
I think this is a very serious problem and I would suggest that where family units are being sponsored to come to this country the age limit for children should be raised from 18 years of age to 21 years of age; that is, providing they are not married. I think this is a matter which I brought to the attention of the minister before, and she was very gracious about it but said that under the regulations there were no provisions to process a case of that kind.
There is also the matter of nieces and nephews. There is no great problem about bringing them into this country from countries like Poland if they are less than 18 years of age; but as soon as they go over the 18 years of age limit you are again faced with the same problem, that there are no provisions in that country to process them. Sometimes you are able to get them through after a great deal of correspondence. Generally speaking, after 18 years of age it is difficult if not impossible to bring them to Canada.
Regarding the bringing to Canada of the children of Chinese families I have often thought that the regulations are a little harsh. They demand the submission of full identification, birth certificates, photographs and things of that nature which are often difficult to obtain. In cases of that sort where a party is bringing young Chinese people to this country the regulations should be

relaxed a little if the sponsoring party is sound financially and a good citizen to make it easier to bring the young people here and unite the families and make them happy.
There are many new Canadians in the Niagara peninsula. In spite of the disappointments experienced in some cases there are hundreds of happily re-united families whose re-union has been made possible through the department. I sincerely appreciate what has been done and thank the minister on their behalf.
I urge the minister and the department to take a second look at the possibility of changing the regulations concerning sponsored immigration where the children are over 18 and concerning the bringing to Canada of nieces and nephews over age 18. I suggest that age 21 should be considered.

Mr. Chairman, I am labouring under difficulties in rising to speak at this time. First, it is five minutes to ten o'clock. Second, I am somewhat timid about hurting a lady's feelings. Third, I have been married for many years, have four daughters and have never yet won an argument with a woman. I trust I will not repeat what has been said although I wish to support and emphasize some comments that have been made.
I am pleased that Dr. Davidson has been appointed deputy minister of the department. Many people wrote me about this. Rather than to proliferate with excessive language it would be simpler for me to quote from an article by Tempus in the June 10 issue of the Financial Times:
The long-delayed shakeup in the department of immigration here is taking place: or has taken place. Laval Fortier, for 10 years the deputy minister of citizenship and immigration, has been moved to the unemployment insurance commission, while Dr. George Davidson, B.S., M.A., Ph.D., moves, after a decade in health and welfare as deputy, to the new post of deputy minister of citizenship and immigration. The Bass river blue-nose-
A nice phrase. I continue:
-is deemed a suitable man for the new policy. After all the trouble Mrs. Ellen Fairclough was having in immigration, heads had to roll: at least one did; not hers.
I do not often agree with Tempus but that is well stated and I believe reflects the view of many Canadians.
I recognize that this department faces problems different from those faced by other departments, problems concerning human beings and problems at times almost intangible through circumstances that arise. Many people have written or spoken to me about immigration problems including veterans, my constituents, members of the
Business of the House
Canadian Legion, officials and members of trade unions and Canadians of Chinese origin residing in my constituency. The latter tell me that regardless of the fact they are represented by one of their own racial origin they prefer to bring their problems to me. I appreciate their point of view very much. They recntly wrote me about their opinion on matters to which I will refer later.
I appreciate the trying tasks the department has to undertake and the difficulties experienced by the staff and officials in coping with regulations that are difficult to administer and with problems arising from the present unplanned immigration policy.
Members of the Canadian Legion and other organizations have asked me to inquire of the minister if all the officials and staff of her department employed since 1945 are entitled to the veterans preference.
I have been ambling along preparatory to coming to the core of my remarks but I see it is thirty seconds to ten o'clock.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker may I inquire what the business is for tomorrow and ask if the house leader could tell us what we will be doing next week?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Tomorrow, Mr. Speaker, we will commence with the estimates of the Department of Transport. If concluded, we have available the estimates of the Post Office Department.
The tentative program for next week is as follows. For Monday and Tuesday there are eight items on the order paper of a legislative nature which will be taken in this order:
1.	The second reading of Bill No. C-74 referring to the Customs Tariff.
2.	Bill No. C-73 referring to the Excise Tax Act.
3.	Bill No. C-65 referring to the Estate Tax Act.
4.	Bill No. C-69 referring to the expenditures of the Canadian National Railways system.
5.	Bill No. C-68 referring to the Income Tax Act.
6.	Bill No. C-64, to amend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act.
7.	Bill No. S-32, to authorize the construction and maintenance of a bridge across the St. Lawrence river near the town of La Salle.
8.	A motion in the name of the Minister of National Revenue to set up a select committee on the subject of broadcasting. That would be called on Tuesday.
For the balance of the week-Wednesday, Thursday and Friday-we will go into committee of supply to consider the estimates in

Business of the House
the following order, subject to adjustment if necessary: the continuation of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, post office, mines and technical surveys, fisheries, veterans affairs, health and welfare. All those are ready. Veterans affairs and health and welfare estimates have both gone to committees and have been carefully studied. The Department of Transport, if not finished tomorrow, will be considered again on Friday of next week.
It being four minutes past ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Friday, June 10, 1960
